questions.title: Catching the cyclist
questions.stem: A cyclist leaves a village at 8:00 a.m., riding at a steady 15 km/h. At 8:40 a.m. a car leaves the same village along the same road, travelling at a steady 55 km/h in the same direction.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: At what time does the car catch up with the cyclist?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How far from the village does this happen?

hints: How far ahead is the cyclist when the car starts? How quickly does the car close that gap?

solution.answer: **(a)** **8:55 a.m.** (b) **13.75 km** from the village.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

When two objects move in the **same direction**, the faster one closes the gap at the **difference** of their speeds. First find the head start, then divide it by that difference.

**Build the reasoning**

**The head start.** By 8:40 the cyclist has ridden for 40 minutes, which is $\frac{2}{3}$ of an hour.

> 15 × $\frac{2}{3}$ = 10 — *kilometres ahead when the car starts*

**Closing speed.**

> 55 − 15 = 40 — *kilometres by which the gap shrinks each hour*\
> 10 ÷ 40 = $\frac{1}{4}$ — *hours to close the gap*

A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes, so the car catches up at 8:55 a.m.

**Distance from the village.** The car has driven for $\frac{1}{4}$ hour:

> 55 × $\frac{1}{4}$ = 13.75 — *kilometres from the village*

**Alternative reasoning**

**Use a table of positions.**

| Time | Cyclist's distance | Car's distance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8:40 | 10 km | 0 km |
| 8:45 | 11.25 km | $4\frac{7}{12}$ km |
| 8:50 | 12.5 km | $9\frac{1}{6}$ km |
| 8:55 | 13.75 km | 13.75 km |

Every 5 minutes the cyclist travels 1.25 km and the car travels $4\frac{7}{12}$ km, so the gap closes by $3\frac{1}{3}$ km every 5 minutes. A 10 km gap closes in 3 lots of 5 minutes.

**Check the answer**

The cyclist rides from 8:00 to 8:55, which is 55 minutes or $\frac{11}{12}$ of an hour: 15 × $\frac{11}{12}$ = 13.75 km. Both are at the same place.

**General lesson**

In a chase, the gap shrinks at the difference of the speeds. Find the gap at the moment the chase starts, then divide by the closing speed.

questions.title: Up the hill and back
questions.stem: Priya cycles up a hill road at a steady 20 km/h and comes straight back down the same road at a steady 30 km/h.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Her friend says Priya's average speed for the whole trip is 25 km/h. Is that right?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find her true average speed.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Explain in words why it is less than 25 km/h.

hints: The length of the road is not given. Choose a convenient length that both 20 and 30 divide into.

solution.answer: **(a)** **No.** (b) **24 km/h.** (c) She spends **more time** going up slowly than coming down quickly, so the slow speed counts for more of the trip's time.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

**Average speed** means total distance ÷ total time: the steady speed that would complete the whole trip in the same total time. It is not the average of the two speeds.

**Find the mathematical structure**

The road length is the same both ways, but the times are different. Since the length is not given, the answer must be the same whatever the length is. So we may choose a convenient length.

**Build the reasoning**

Choose the road to be 60 km long (60 is divisible by both 20 and 30).

> 60 ÷ 20 = 3 — *hours going up*\
> 60 ÷ 30 = 2 — *hours coming down*\
> 60 + 60 = 120 — *kilometres in total*\
> 3 + 2 = 5 — *hours in total*\
> 120 ÷ 5 = 24 — *kilometres per hour on average*

**Alternative reasoning**

**Check that the length does not matter.** Try a 6 km road: 0.3 hours up and 0.2 hours down, so 12 km in 0.5 hours, which is again 24 km/h. In general each kilometre of road takes $\frac{1}{20}$ hour up and $\frac{1}{30}$ hour down. So 2 km of riding (1 km up and 1 km down) takes:

> $\frac{1}{20}$ + $\frac{1}{30}$ = $\frac{1}{12}$ — *hours for 1 km up and 1 km down*\
> 2 ÷ $\frac{1}{12}$ = 24 — *kilometres per hour*

**Develop intuition**

On the 60 km road, Priya rides for 3 hours at 20 km/h but only 2 hours at 30 km/h. If you average the speed over each hour of the trip, three hours "vote" for 20 and only two hours "vote" for 30: (3 × 20 + 2 × 30) ÷ 5 = 120 ÷ 5 = 24.

**Check the answer**

The average must lie between 20 and 30, and closer to 20, because more time is spent at 20 km/h. 24 is closer to 20 than 25 is.

**General lesson**

Average speed is total distance ÷ total time. Averaging the two speeds works only when equal **times** are spent at each speed, not equal distances.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: An average that cannot be reached
questions.stem: A driver must cover a 2 km stretch of road. She drives the first kilometre at a steady 30 km/h. How fast must she drive the second kilometre so that her average speed for the whole 2 km is 60 km/h?
hints: How much time is allowed for the whole 2 km at an average of 60 km/h? How much has she already used?

solution.answer: **It is impossible.** To average 60 km/h over 2 km she must finish in 2 minutes, but the first kilometre alone has already taken 2 minutes. However fast she drives the second kilometre, she cannot do it in no time at all.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

"Average 60 km/h over 2 km" is a statement about the **total time**: it fixes how long the whole trip may take. The first kilometre has used up part of that time.

**Build the reasoning**

**Time allowed for the whole trip.** At 60 km/h she covers 1 km every minute.

> 2 ÷ 60 × 60 = 2 — *minutes allowed for 2 km*

**Time already used.** At 30 km/h she covers 1 km in 2 minutes.

> 1 ÷ 30 × 60 = 2 — *minutes used for the first kilometre*\
> 2 − 2 = 0 — *minutes left for the second kilometre*

No speed covers a kilometre in 0 minutes.

**How close can she get?**

| Speed on 2nd km | Time on 2nd km | Total time | Average speed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 60 km/h | 1 min | 3 min | 40 km/h |
| 120 km/h | 0.5 min | 2.5 min | 48 km/h |
| 600 km/h | 0.1 min | 2.1 min | about 57.1 km/h |

The average creeps towards 60 km/h as the second speed grows, but it never reaches it.

**Develop intuition**

The time allowed for the whole 2 km is 2 minutes, and the first kilometre has already used all of it. Driving the second kilometre faster only shrinks its time towards 0 minutes, never all the way to 0, so the total time is always more than 2 minutes.

**Check the answer**

The tempting answer is 90 km/h, because (30 + 90) ÷ 2 = 60. But at 90 km/h the second kilometre takes $\frac{2}{3}$ of a minute, so the total time is $2\frac{2}{3}$ minutes and the average speed is 2 ÷ $2\frac{2}{3}$ × 60 = 45 km/h.

**General lesson**

An average speed fixes the total time. When the time is already used up, no later speed can fix it. Always translate an average-speed target into a time budget.

questions.answer: **It is impossible.** To average 60 km/h over 2 km she must finish in 2 minutes, but the first kilometre alone has already taken 2 minutes. However fast she drives the second kilometre, she cannot do it in no time at all.
