questions.title: Twice as fast
questions.stem: Asha works twice as fast as Bilal, and each of them works at a steady rate. Working together, they finish a job in 12 days. How long would each of them take to do the job alone?
hints: Think of Asha as being worth two Bilals.

solution.answer: **Asha: 18 days. Bilal: 36 days.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Asha does twice as much as Bilal in any day. So the pair works like **three Bilals**. Using the job's size in "Bilal-days" turns the problem into ordinary inverse proportion.

**Build the reasoning**

Asha and Bilal together are equivalent to 3 Bilals, and 3 Bilals take 12 days.

> 3 × 12 = 36 — *Bilal-days in the job*

So Bilal alone takes 36 days. Asha works twice as fast, so she takes half as long:

> 36 ÷ 2 = 18 — *days for Asha alone*

**Alternative reasoning**

**With rates.** Suppose Bilal does a fraction *r* of the job each day; then Asha does 2 × *r*. Together they do 3 × *r* each day, which must be $\frac{1}{12}$ of the job.

> $\frac{1}{12}$ ÷ 3 = $\frac{1}{36}$ — *of the job done by Bilal each day*\
> 2 × $\frac{1}{36}$ = $\frac{1}{18}$ — *of the job done by Asha each day*

**Check the answer**

$\frac{1}{18}$ + $\frac{1}{36}$ = $\frac{2}{36}$ + $\frac{1}{36}$ = $\frac{3}{36}$ = $\frac{1}{12}$, so together they do $\frac{1}{12}$ of the job each day and finish in 12 days.

**General lesson**

When workers differ in speed, measure everyone in units of the slowest (or any one) worker. The problem then becomes an ordinary inverse-proportion problem.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: One worker leaves
questions.stem: Ravi can do a job alone in 10 days. Sunita can do the same job alone in 15 days. They work together for 4 days, and then Ravi leaves. Each works at a steady rate.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How much of the job is done after the first 4 days?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How many more days does Sunita need to finish?

parts.label: c
parts.stem: How many days does the whole job take?

hints: Split the story into two stages: together, then Sunita alone.

solution.answer: **(a)** **$\frac{2}{3}$** of the job. (b) **5 more days.** (c) **9 days** in total.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Stage 1:** both work, so their rates add.
- **Stage 2:** only Sunita works, at her own rate, on what is left.
- The stages happen one after the other, so their **times add**.

**Build the reasoning**

**Stage 1.**

> $\frac{1}{10}$ + $\frac{1}{15}$ = $\frac{1}{6}$ — *of the job done each day together*\
> 4 × $\frac{1}{6}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ — *of the job done in 4 days*

**Stage 2.**

> 1 − $\frac{2}{3}$ = $\frac{1}{3}$ — *of the job left*\
> $\frac{1}{3}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{15}$ = 5 — *days for Sunita to finish*

**Total.**

> 4 + 5 = 9 — *days altogether*

**Alternative reasoning**

Pretend the job is 30 units (30 is the smallest number that 10 and 15 divide). Ravi does 3 units per day and Sunita 2 units per day. In 4 days together they do 4 × 5 = 20 units. The remaining 10 units take Sunita 10 ÷ 2 = 5 days.

**Check the answer**

Over 9 days, Sunita works all 9 days and does $\frac{9}{15}$ of the job; Ravi works 4 days and does $\frac{4}{10}$ of it. $\frac{9}{15}$ + $\frac{4}{10}$ = $\frac{3}{5}$ + $\frac{2}{5}$ = 1 whole job.

**General lesson**

Rates add for agents working at the same time; times add for stages that happen one after another. In staged problems, find the work done in each stage and keep track of what remains.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Two pipes and a drain
questions.stem: Pipe A alone can fill a tank in 12 hours, and pipe B alone can fill it in 15 hours. Drain C alone can empty the full tank in 20 hours. All three are opened when the tank is empty, and they work at steady rates. How long does the tank take to fill?
hints: Pretend the tank holds a number of buckets that 12, 15 and 20 all divide into.

solution.answer: **10 hours.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

The two pipes add water and the drain removes it, all at the same time. Net rate = rate of A + rate of B − rate of C.

**Build the reasoning**

> $\frac{1}{12}$ + $\frac{1}{15}$ − $\frac{1}{20}$ = $\frac{1}{10}$ — *of the tank gained each hour*

Write the fractions with the common denominator 60 to see this: $\frac{5}{60}$ + $\frac{4}{60}$ − $\frac{3}{60}$ = $\frac{6}{60}$ = $\frac{1}{10}$.

> 1 ÷ $\frac{1}{10}$ = 10 — *hours to fill the tank*

**Alternative reasoning**

**Convenient units.** 60 is the smallest number divisible by 12, 15 and 20, so pretend the tank holds 60 buckets.

> 60 ÷ 12 = 5 — *buckets per hour from A*\
> 60 ÷ 15 = 4 — *buckets per hour from B*\
> 60 ÷ 20 = 3 — *buckets per hour lost through C*\
> 5 + 4 − 3 = 6 — *buckets gained per hour*\
> 60 ÷ 6 = 10 — *hours*

**Check the answer**

In 10 hours: A adds $\frac{10}{12}$ of a tank, B adds $\frac{10}{15}$, and C removes $\frac{10}{20}$. $\frac{5}{6}$ + $\frac{2}{3}$ − $\frac{1}{2}$ = $\frac{5}{6}$ + $\frac{4}{6}$ − $\frac{3}{6}$ = 1 whole tank.

**General lesson**

With several agents, convert each into a rate (positive for filling, negative for emptying) and add them. A convenient number of units, often the least common multiple of the times, avoids fractions.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: The second pipe alone
questions.stem: Two pipes working together fill an empty swimming pool in 6 hours. The first pipe alone would fill it in 10 hours. How long would the second pipe alone take? Both pipes flow at steady rates.
hints: In one hour, the two pipes fill $\frac{1}{6}$ of the pool. How much of that is from the first pipe?

solution.answer: **15 hours.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Combined rate = rate of first pipe + rate of second pipe. We know the combined rate and the first rate, so we subtract.

**Build the reasoning**

> $\frac{1}{6}$ − $\frac{1}{10}$ = $\frac{1}{15}$ — *of the pool filled each hour by the second pipe*\
> 1 ÷ $\frac{1}{15}$ = 15 — *hours for the second pipe alone*

**Alternative reasoning**

Pretend the pool holds 30 units. Together the pipes add 30 ÷ 6 = 5 units per hour, and the first pipe adds 30 ÷ 10 = 3 units per hour. So the second pipe adds 2 units per hour and needs 30 ÷ 2 = 15 hours.

**Check the answer**

- $\frac{1}{10}$ + $\frac{1}{15}$ = $\frac{3}{30}$ + $\frac{2}{30}$ = $\frac{5}{30}$ = $\frac{1}{6}$, so the two pipes together do fill the pool in 6 hours.
- The second pipe must be slower than the pair (more than 6 hours). It is also slower than the first pipe, because together they take more than half of the first pipe's 10 hours.

**General lesson**

To find one agent's rate from a combined rate, subtract the known rates. Work in rates, then turn the final rate back into a time.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Overtaking on parallel tracks
questions.stem: A train 200 m long travels at a steady 72 km/h. On a parallel track, in the same direction, a train 100 m long travels at a steady 54 km/h.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long does overtaking take, from the moment the front of the faster train reaches the back of the slower train until the back of the faster train passes the front of the slower train?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: If the two trains were travelling in **opposite** directions at the same speeds, how long would they take to pass each other completely, from the moment their fronts meet until their backs separate?

hints: How far must the faster train move **relative to** the slower one, and how fast does it gain on it?

solution.answer: **(a)** **60 seconds.** (b) $8\frac{4}{7}$ seconds (about 8.6 seconds).
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

During overtaking, what matters is how the faster train moves **compared with** the slower one. From the point of view of a passenger on the slower train, the faster train creeps forward at the difference of the speeds.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Distance to be gained: at the start, the faster train's front is level with the slower train's back, so its own back is 200 m further behind. At the end, its back is level with the slower train's front, which is 100 m ahead of the slower train's back. Compared with the slower train, it must move 200 + 100 = 300 m: the **sum of the two lengths**.
- Same direction: relative speed = difference of speeds. Opposite directions: relative speed = sum of speeds.

**Build the reasoning**

**Convert the speeds to metres per second.** Each km/h is $\frac{1000}{3600}$ = $\frac{5}{18}$ m/s.

> 72 × $\frac{5}{18}$ = 20 — *metres per second*\
> 54 × $\frac{5}{18}$ = 15 — *metres per second*

**(a)**

> 20 − 15 = 5 — *metres per second gained by the faster train*\
> 200 + 100 = 300 — *metres to be gained*\
> 300 ÷ 5 = 60 — *seconds*

**(b)**

> 20 + 15 = 35 — *metres per second closing speed*\
> 300 ÷ 35 = $8\frac{4}{7}$ — *seconds*

**Develop intuition**

Watch the trains from the slower train. It seems to stand still, and the faster train slides past at a gentle 5 m/s. Overtaking means sliding a whole 300 m: from "the fast train's front at the slow train's back" to "the fast train's back at the slow train's front".

**Check the answer**

In 60 seconds the faster train covers 1,200 m and the slower train covers 900 m. The difference, 300 m, is exactly the sum of their lengths.

**General lesson**

When objects with length pass each other, the distance is the sum of their lengths, and the speed is the relative speed: the difference for the same direction, the sum for opposite directions.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Walking up the escalator
questions.stem: Ira stands still on a moving escalator and is carried from the bottom to the top in 60 seconds. When the escalator is switched off, she walks up it in 90 seconds. How long does she take if she walks up the moving escalator at her usual pace?
hints: In one second, what fraction of the escalator does the machine carry her? What fraction do her legs carry her?

solution.answer: **36 seconds.**
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

When Ira walks on the moving escalator, two things move her up at the same time: the escalator and her own legs. This is a work problem in disguise, where the "job" is covering the length of the escalator.

**Find the mathematical structure**

The two contributions happen at the same time, so their rates add:

- the escalator carries her $\frac{1}{60}$ of the way each second;
- walking carries her $\frac{1}{90}$ of the way each second.

**Build the reasoning**

> $\frac{1}{60}$ + $\frac{1}{90}$ = $\frac{1}{36}$ — *of the escalator covered each second*\
> 1 ÷ $\frac{1}{36}$ = 36 — *seconds*

**Alternative reasoning**

Pretend the escalator has 180 steps (180 is divisible by 60 and 90). The machine moves her 3 steps per second and her legs move her 2 steps per second. Together, 5 steps per second, so 180 steps take 36 seconds.

**Check the answer**

The answer must be less than 60 seconds (faster than standing) and more than 30 seconds (two copies of the faster rate would take 60 ÷ 2 = 30 seconds). 36 seconds fits.

**General lesson**

Combined-rate thinking applies to motion too. Any two effects that act at the same time, such as an escalator and walking, or a river and rowing, add their rates.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: A boat on a river
questions.stem: A boat travels 24 km downstream in 2 hours, and then returns the same 24 km upstream in 3 hours. The boat's speed through the water and the river's current are both steady.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the boat's speed in still water and the speed of the current.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How long would a log, floating with the current, take to drift 24 km downstream?

hints: Downstream, the current helps the boat; upstream, it holds it back. What are the two actual speeds?

solution.answer: **(a)** The boat's speed in still water is **10 km/h** and the current is **2 km/h**. (b) **12 hours.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

- Downstream speed = boat speed + current speed.
- Upstream speed = boat speed − current speed.

The current adds on the way down and subtracts on the way up by the same amount.

**Build the reasoning**

> 24 ÷ 2 = 12 — *km/h downstream*\
> 24 ÷ 3 = 8 — *km/h upstream*

The difference between these two speeds is twice the current, because the current is added once and subtracted once:

> (12 − 8) ÷ 2 = 2 — *km/h, the current*\
> 12 − 2 = 10 — *km/h, the boat in still water*

**(b)** The log has no engine, so it moves at the speed of the current alone:

> 24 ÷ 2 = 12 — *hours*

**Develop intuition**

The boat's speed in still water lies exactly halfway between its downstream and upstream speeds: (12 + 8) ÷ 2 = 10 km/h. The current is the distance from that midpoint to either speed.

**Check the answer**

10 + 2 = 12 km/h, which covers 24 km in 2 hours. 10 − 2 = 8 km/h, which covers 24 km in 3 hours.

**General lesson**

When a steady effect (a current, a wind) helps one way and hinders the other, the average of the two speeds removes it, and half their difference measures it.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Two cooks and 150 rotis
questions.stem: Cook A makes 30 rotis in 10 minutes. Cook B makes 30 rotis in 15 minutes. They work together at these steady rates.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long do they take to make 150 rotis?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How many of the 150 rotis does each cook make?

hints: How many rotis does each cook make in one minute?

solution.answer: **(a)** **30 minutes.** (b) Cook A makes **90** rotis and Cook B makes **60**.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

This time the rates are counts per minute ("rotis per minute"), not fractions of a job. The idea is the same: working at the same time, their rates add.

**Build the reasoning**

> 30 ÷ 10 = 3 — *rotis per minute from Cook A*\
> 30 ÷ 15 = 2 — *rotis per minute from Cook B*\
> 3 + 2 = 5 — *rotis per minute together*\
> 150 ÷ 5 = 30 — *minutes for 150 rotis*

**(b)** Both cooks work the full 30 minutes:

> 3 × 30 = 90 — *rotis made by Cook A*\
> 2 × 30 = 60 — *rotis made by Cook B*

**Alternative reasoning**

**Treat it as a fraction-of-a-job problem.** Cook A alone would make 150 rotis in 50 minutes, and Cook B alone in 75 minutes. Together they make $\frac{1}{50}$ + $\frac{1}{75}$ = $\frac{3}{150}$ + $\frac{2}{150}$ = $\frac{5}{150}$ = $\frac{1}{30}$ of the order each minute, so 30 minutes. Counting rotis directly was simpler here.

**Check the answer**

90 + 60 = 150. Also, Cook A works $\frac{3}{2}$ times as fast as Cook B, and 90 is $\frac{3}{2}$ of 60.

**General lesson**

Rates can be counts per unit of time or fractions of a job per unit of time. Choose whichever makes the arithmetic simpler. Work shared in a fixed time is split in the ratio of the rates.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Taking turns with the taps
questions.stem: Tap A alone fills a tank in 4 hours; tap B alone fills it in 6 hours. Starting with the tank empty, tap A is opened on its own for 1 hour, then tap B on its own for 1 hour, then A for 1 hour, and so on, switching every hour. Only one tap is ever open.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long does the tank take to fill?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: A student says: "Each 2 hours, the taps fill $\frac{1}{4}$ + $\frac{1}{6}$ = $\frac{5}{12}$ of the tank, so the tank takes $\frac{24}{5}$ hours, which is 4 hours 48 minutes." Find the flaw.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: If tap B were opened first instead, would the tank take the same time to fill?

hints: Keep a running total of the fraction filled, hour by hour. Watch carefully what happens in the last hour.

solution.answer:
**(a)** **4 hours 40 minutes.**

**(b)** The student assumes the tank fills at an **average** rate right to the end. But the last part is filled by tap A alone, which is faster than the average, so it finishes sooner.

**(c)** **No.** Starting with B, the tank takes exactly **5 hours**.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

The taps take turns, so in each hour only one rate applies. The pattern repeats every 2 hours, but the final stage must be calculated with the rate of whichever tap is running when the tank becomes full.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)** Keep a running total.

| Hour | Tap open | Filled in that hour | Total filled |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st | A | $\frac{3}{12}$ | $\frac{3}{12}$ |
| 2nd | B | $\frac{2}{12}$ | $\frac{5}{12}$ |
| 3rd | A | $\frac{3}{12}$ | $\frac{8}{12}$ |
| 4th | B | $\frac{2}{12}$ | $\frac{10}{12}$ |

After 4 hours, $\frac{10}{12}$ = $\frac{5}{6}$ of the tank is full. In the 5th hour tap A is open, and only $\frac{1}{6}$ of the tank remains.

> $\frac{1}{6}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{4}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ — *hour for tap A to fill the last sixth*

$\frac{2}{3}$ of an hour is 40 minutes, so the tank is full after 4 hours 40 minutes.

**(c)** Starting with B, the running totals after each hour are $\frac{2}{12}$, $\frac{5}{12}$, $\frac{7}{12}$, $\frac{10}{12}$. In the 5th hour tap B is open and must fill the last $\frac{2}{12}$ = $\frac{1}{6}$:

> $\frac{1}{6}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{6}$ = 1 — *hour for tap B*

So the tank is full after exactly 5 hours.

**Develop intuition**

The two orders give the same total after every even number of hours, but whichever tap gets the last turn decides how quickly the final bit is filled. Starting with the faster tap gives it the last turn here.

**Check the answer**

In (a), tap A runs for 1 + 1 + $\frac{2}{3}$ = $\frac{8}{3}$ hours, filling $\frac{8}{3}$ × $\frac{1}{4}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ of the tank, and tap B runs for 2 hours, filling $\frac{2}{6}$ = $\frac{1}{3}$. Total: 1 tank.

**General lesson**

An average rate is safe only when the process runs in complete cycles. When the job ends part-way through a cycle, finish the calculation with the actual rate of the final stage.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Three journeys, three averages
questions.stem:
A car makes three different journeys.

- Journey 1: 2 hours at 60 km/h, then 3 hours at 80 km/h.
- Journey 2: 1 hour at 60 km/h, then 1 hour at 80 km/h.
- Journey 3: 120 km at 60 km/h, then 120 km at 80 km/h.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the average speed for each journey.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: For which journey does "add the two speeds and halve" give the correct average speed? Explain why it works for that journey and not the others.

hints: For every journey, find the total distance and the total time.

solution.answer:
**(a)** Journey 1: **72 km/h**. Journey 2: **70 km/h**. Journey 3: $68\frac{4}{7}$ km/h (about **68.6 km/h**).

**(b)** Only **Journey 2**, where the car spends **equal times** at each speed.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, in every case. The question is how much **time** is spent at each speed.

**Build the reasoning**

**Journey 1.**

> 60 × 2 + 80 × 3 = 360 — *kilometres*\
> 360 ÷ 5 = 72 — *km/h average*

**Journey 2.**

> 60 + 80 = 140 — *kilometres in 2 hours*\
> 140 ÷ 2 = 70 — *km/h average*

**Journey 3.**

> 120 ÷ 60 + 120 ÷ 80 = 3.5 — *hours in total*\
> 240 ÷ 3.5 = $68\frac{4}{7}$ — *km/h average*

**Why equal times matter**

Think of the average speed as the average over every **minute** of the journey. In Journey 2, half the minutes are spent at 60 km/h and half at 80 km/h, so the simple average 70 km/h is right. In Journey 1, more minutes are spent at 80 km/h, so the average is pulled above 70. In Journey 3, the distances are equal, so more minutes are spent at the slower speed (2 hours against 1.5 hours), pulling the average below 70.

**Check the answer**

All three averages lie between 60 and 80 km/h, as they must. The equal-distance journey has the lowest average, which matches the hill problem: equal distances favour the slow part.

**General lesson**

"Add and halve" is correct only for equal times. For anything else, compute total distance ÷ total time.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Runners on a circular track
questions.stem: Arun and Bela start together from the same point on a 400 m circular track. Arun runs at a steady 5 m/s and Bela at a steady 3 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: If they run in the same direction, after how many seconds does Arun first catch up with Bela again?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: If they run in opposite directions, after how many seconds do they first meet?

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Running in opposite directions, how many times do they meet in the first 10 minutes? Do not count the start, but do count a meeting at exactly 10 minutes.

hints: In (a), how much further than Bela must Arun run to catch her? In (b), how much track must they cover between them?

solution.answer: **(a)** **200 seconds.** (b) **50 seconds.** (c) **12 times.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

- Same direction: Arun gains on Bela at 5 − 3 = 2 m/s. To catch her he must gain one full lap, 400 m.
- Opposite directions: together they cover 5 + 3 = 8 m of track each second. They meet each time they have covered a full lap, 400 m, between them.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)**

> 5 − 3 = 2 — *metres per second gained by Arun*\
> 400 ÷ 2 = 200 — *seconds to gain a full lap*

**(b)**

> 5 + 3 = 8 — *metres per second covered between them*\
> 400 ÷ 8 = 50 — *seconds until they first meet*

**(c)** They meet every 50 seconds. 10 minutes is 600 seconds.

> 600 ÷ 50 = 12 — *meetings, the last one at exactly 600 seconds*

**Check the answer**

- (a) In 200 seconds Arun runs 1,000 m (2.5 laps) and Bela runs 600 m (1.5 laps). Arun is exactly one lap ahead, so they are side by side.
- (b) In 50 seconds Arun runs 250 m one way and Bela 150 m the other way: 250 + 150 = 400 m, the whole track.

**General lesson**

On a circular track, "catching up" means gaining a whole lap at the difference of the speeds, and "meeting head-on" means covering a whole lap between you at the sum of the speeds.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: When the clock hands meet
questions.stem: At 3:00 the minute hand of a clock points at 12 and the hour hand points at 3. Both hands turn at steady rates.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How many degrees does each hand turn in one minute?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: At what time after 3:00 are the two hands first exactly on top of each other? Give the time to the nearest second.

hints: A full turn is 360°. The minute hand makes one full turn every 60 minutes; the hour hand makes one full turn every 12 hours. Then this is a catching-up problem.

solution.answer:
**(a)** The minute hand turns **6°** per minute; the hour hand turns **0.5°** per minute.

**(b)** $16\frac{4}{11}$ minutes after 3:00, which is about **3:16:22**.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The minute hand is chasing the hour hand around the clock face. At 3:00 the hour hand is 90° ahead (a quarter of a turn), and the minute hand turns faster, so it catches up.

**Find the mathematical structure**

This is a catching-up problem with angles instead of kilometres: the gap of 90° closes at the **difference** of the two turning rates.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)**

> 360 ÷ 60 = 6 — *degrees per minute for the minute hand*\
> 360 ÷ (12 × 60) = 0.5 — *degrees per minute for the hour hand*

**(b)**

> 6 − 0.5 = 5.5 — *degrees per minute by which the gap closes*\
> 90 ÷ 5.5 = $16\frac{4}{11}$ — *minutes after 3:00*

Convert the fraction of a minute into seconds:

> $\frac{4}{11}$ × 60 = $21\frac{9}{11}$ — *seconds, about 21.8 seconds*

To the nearest second, the hands meet at 3:16:22.

**Check the answer**

In $16\frac{4}{11}$ minutes the minute hand turns 6 × $16\frac{4}{11}$ = $98\frac{2}{11}$°, and the hour hand turns 0.5 × $16\frac{4}{11}$ = $8\frac{2}{11}$°, ending at 90° + $8\frac{2}{11}$° = $98\frac{2}{11}$° from 12. Both hands point in the same direction.

**Develop intuition**

The answer is a little after 3:15, not exactly 3:15, because while the minute hand travels to the 3, the hour hand has crept forward a little.

**General lesson**

Relative speed is not only for vehicles. Any chase, including two hands on a clock, closes the gap at the difference of the rates.

fields.Section: Combined rates: work, pipes, leaks, speed and average speed

questions.title: Toys from the workshop
questions.stem: 12 workers make 360 toys in 5 days. How many toys will 18 workers make in 8 days? All the workers work at the same steady rate.
hints: How many toys does one worker make in one day?

solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

Two things change at once: the number of workers and the number of days. Both changes increase the output.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Output depends on **workers** and on **days**. More workers make more toys; more days make more toys.
- The natural unit is the **worker-day**: the work of one worker for one day. Output = (toys per worker-day) × (worker-days).
- Assumptions: every worker is equally fast, and the rate does not change from day to day.

**Build the reasoning**

**Method 1: through one worker-day.**

> 12 × 5 = 60 — *worker-days in the first situation*\
> 360 ÷ 60 = 6 — *toys made in each worker-day*\
> 18 × 8 = 144 — *worker-days in the new situation*\
> 144 × 6 = 864 — *toys*

**Method 2: one change at a time.**

- More workers, 12 → 18: output is multiplied by $\frac{18}{12}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$.
- More days, 5 → 8: output is multiplied by $\frac{8}{5}$.

> 360 × $\frac{3}{2}$ × $\frac{8}{5}$ = 864 — *toys*

**Develop intuition**

Picture a grid with one square for each worker on each day. The first situation has 12 × 5 = 60 squares and produces 360 toys, so each square produces 6 toys. The new grid has 18 × 8 = 144 squares.

**Check the answer**

Both changes push the output up, and 864 is much more than 360. Increasing the workers by half and the days by more than half should more than double the output: 864 is 2.4 times 360, and $\frac{3}{2}$ × $\frac{8}{5}$ = 2.4.

**General lesson**

When output depends on several quantities, either combine them into one unit (worker-days) or change one quantity at a time and multiply the factors. Both methods give the same answer.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Machines making bolts
questions.stem: 10 identical machines working 8 hours a day produce 4,000 bolts in 5 days. How many days will 8 of these machines, working 10 hours a day, take to produce 6,000 bolts? Each machine works at a steady rate.
hints: How many bolts does one machine make in one hour?

solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

- The number of days depends on three things: the number of machines, the hours per day and the number of bolts.
- More machines or more hours per day mean **fewer** days. More bolts mean **more** days.
- The combined unit is the **machine-hour**: one machine running for one hour.

**Build the reasoning**

**Method 1: machine-hours.**

> 10 × 8 × 5 = 400 — *machine-hours in the first situation*\
> 4,000 ÷ 400 = 10 — *bolts per machine-hour*\
> 6,000 ÷ 10 = 600 — *machine-hours needed for 6,000 bolts*\
> 8 × 10 = 80 — *machine-hours available each day in the new situation*\
> 600 ÷ 80 = 7.5 — *days*

**Method 2: one change at a time,** starting from 5 days.

- Machines 10 → 8: fewer machines, so more days. Multiply by $\frac{10}{8}$.
- Hours per day 8 → 10: longer days, so fewer days. Multiply by $\frac{8}{10}$.
- Bolts 4,000 → 6,000: more bolts, so more days. Multiply by $\frac{6000}{4000}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$.

> 5 × $\frac{10}{8}$ × $\frac{8}{10}$ × $\frac{3}{2}$ = 7.5 — *days*

**Develop intuition**

The first two changes cancel exactly: 8 machines for 10 hours a day give the same 80 machine-hours per day as 10 machines for 8 hours a day. Only the larger order matters, and 1.5 times the bolts take 1.5 times as long: 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 days.

**Check the answer**

8 machines × 10 hours × 7.5 days = 600 machine-hours, and 600 × 10 = 6,000 bolts.

**General lesson**

Predict the direction of each change before writing its factor. Factors that make the answer bigger are greater than 1; factors that make it smaller are less than 1. Combined units such as machine-hours often reveal that some changes cancel.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Rice for a group
questions.stem: 15 people eat 45 kg of rice in 6 days. For how many days will 60 kg of rice last 20 people, if everyone eats the same amount each day?
hints: How much rice does one person eat in one day?

solution.answer: **6 days.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Rice eaten = (rice per person-day) × (number of people) × (number of days). One **person-day** is one person eating for one day.

**Build the reasoning**

> 15 × 6 = 90 — *person-days in the first situation*\
> 45 ÷ 90 = 0.5 — *kilograms of rice per person-day*\
> 60 ÷ 0.5 = 120 — *person-days of rice in 60 kg*\
> 120 ÷ 20 = 6 — *days for 20 people*

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time**, starting from 6 days:

- more rice (45 → 60 kg): more days, multiply by $\frac{60}{45}$ = $\frac{4}{3}$;
- more people (15 → 20): fewer days, multiply by $\frac{15}{20}$ = $\frac{3}{4}$.

> 6 × $\frac{4}{3}$ × $\frac{3}{4}$ = 6 — *days*

The two changes cancel: a third more rice is shared among a third more people.

**Check the answer**

20 people × 6 days × 0.5 kg = 60 kg.

**General lesson**

Find the amount used per person-day, then share the new supply. Opposite changes of the same size cancel.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Pumps and a bigger tank
questions.stem:
6 identical pumps, each working at a steady rate, empty a 9,000-litre tank in 5 hours. How long will 4 such pumps take to empty a 12,000-litre tank?

Before calculating, predict whether each change (fewer pumps, more water) makes the time longer or shorter, and by what factor.
hints: Fewer pumps: longer or shorter? More water: longer or shorter? Write a factor for each.

solution.answer: Both changes make the time **longer**: fewer pumps multiply the time by $\frac{6}{4}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$, and more water multiplies it by $\frac{12}{9}$ = $\frac{4}{3}$. The time is **10 hours**.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Time is inversely proportional to the number of pumps and directly proportional to the amount of water, assuming every pump removes water at the same steady rate.

**Build the reasoning**

**One change at a time:**

> 5 × $\frac{6}{4}$ = 7.5 — *hours for 4 pumps on the 9,000-litre tank*\
> 7.5 × $\frac{12}{9}$ = 10 — *hours for 4 pumps on the 12,000-litre tank*

**Check with pump-hours:**

> 6 × 5 = 30 — *pump-hours to remove 9,000 litres*\
> 9,000 ÷ 30 = 300 — *litres per pump-hour*\
> 12,000 ÷ (4 × 300) = 10 — *hours*

**Check the answer**

Both factors are greater than 1, so the answer must be more than 5 hours. It is: 5 × $\frac{3}{2}$ × $\frac{4}{3}$ = 5 × 2 = 10.

**General lesson**

Predicting directions first protects you from upside-down factors. If both changes make the job harder, the answer must grow.

questions.answer: Both changes make the time **longer**: fewer pumps multiply the time by $\frac{6}{4}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$, and more water multiplies it by $\frac{12}{9}$ = $\frac{4}{3}$. The time is **10 hours**.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Laying a road
questions.stem: 9 workers, working 8 hours a day, lay 1.2 km of road in 10 days. How many workers, working 6 hours a day, are needed to lay 1.5 km of road in 15 days? Assume all workers work at the same steady rate.
hints: How many worker-hours does one kilometre of road need?

solution.answer: **10 workers.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

The unknown is the number of workers. The job is measured in **worker-hours**: one worker working for one hour. Each new worker contributes (hours per day) × (days) worker-hours.

**Build the reasoning**

> 9 × 8 × 10 = 720 — *worker-hours to lay 1.2 km*\
> 720 ÷ 1.2 = 600 — *worker-hours for each kilometre*\
> 1.5 × 600 = 900 — *worker-hours to lay 1.5 km*\
> 6 × 15 = 90 — *hours that each new worker works*\
> 900 ÷ 90 = 10 — *workers*

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time**, starting from 9 workers:

- longer road (1.2 → 1.5 km): more workers, multiply by $\frac{1.5}{1.2}$ = $\frac{5}{4}$;
- shorter working day (8 → 6 hours): more workers, multiply by $\frac{8}{6}$ = $\frac{4}{3}$;
- more days (10 → 15): fewer workers, multiply by $\frac{10}{15}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$.

> 9 × $\frac{5}{4}$ × $\frac{4}{3}$ × $\frac{2}{3}$ = 10 — *workers*

**Check the answer**

10 workers × 6 hours × 15 days = 900 worker-hours, which lays 900 ÷ 600 = 1.5 km.

**General lesson**

In a compound problem the unknown can be any of the quantities. Measure the whole job in a combined unit, then divide by what each unit of the unknown contributes.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Cats and mice
questions.stem:
5 cats catch 5 mice in 5 minutes. How many cats are needed to catch 100 mice in 100 minutes? Assume every cat catches mice at the same steady rate, and there are always mice to catch.

Most people's first answer is 100 cats. Find the correct answer and explain exactly what is wrong with 100.
hints: How many mice does **one** cat catch in 5 minutes? And in 100 minutes?

solution.answer: **5 cats.** The answer 100 scales the number of cats up with the number of mice but forgets that the cats also get 20 times as long to catch them.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Mice caught = (mice per cat-minute) × (cats) × (minutes). Two quantities change: the number of mice (×20) and the time (×20). More mice need more cats, but more time needs fewer cats.

**Build the reasoning**

**Through one cat.** 5 cats catch 5 mice in 5 minutes, so each cat catches 1 mouse in 5 minutes.

> 100 ÷ 5 = 20 — *periods of 5 minutes in 100 minutes*\
> 20 × 1 = 20 — *mice caught by one cat in 100 minutes*\
> 100 ÷ 20 = 5 — *cats needed for 100 mice*

**One change at a time**, starting from 5 cats:

- 20 times as many mice: multiply the cats by 20.
- 20 times as long: divide the cats by 20.

> 5 × 20 ÷ 20 = 5 — *cats*

**Develop intuition**

Nothing about the situation needs more cats. The same 5 cats simply keep hunting. In every 5 minutes they catch 5 more mice, and after 20 such periods they have caught 100.

**Check the answer**

Cat-minutes: 5 cats × 5 minutes = 25 cat-minutes per 5 mice, so 5 cat-minutes per mouse. 100 mice need 500 cat-minutes, and 500 ÷ 100 minutes = 5 cats.

**General lesson**

In compound problems, every quantity that changes must be accounted for. The answer "100" responds to the change in mice but ignores the change in time.

questions.answer: **5 cats.** The answer 100 scales the number of cats up with the number of mice but forgets that the cats also get 20 times as long to catch them.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Tailors and trainees
questions.stem: A school orders new uniforms. 6 experienced tailors can stitch the whole order in 15 days, or 10 trainee tailors can stitch the same order in 15 days. All the experienced tailors work at the same rate as each other, and all the trainees work at the same rate as each other.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long will 3 experienced tailors and 5 trainees take, working together?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How long will 3 experienced tailors and 4 trainees take?

hints: 6 experienced tailors do the same work in a day as 10 trainees. How many trainees is one experienced tailor worth?

solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Because 6 experienced tailors and 10 trainees do the same work in a day, we can convert everyone into a common unit: **trainee-equivalents**. One experienced tailor = $\frac{10}{6}$ = $\frac{5}{3}$ trainees. Then the team is an ordinary number of identical workers.

**Build the reasoning**

**The job in trainee-days:**

> 10 × 15 = 150 — *trainee-days of work*

**(a)**

> 3 × $\frac{5}{3}$ = 5 — *trainee-equivalents from 3 experienced tailors*\
> 5 + 5 = 10 — *trainee-equivalents in the team*\
> 150 ÷ 10 = 15 — *days*

**(b)**

> 5 + 4 = 9 — *trainee-equivalents in the team*\
> 150 ÷ 9 = $16\frac{2}{3}$ — *days*

**Develop intuition**

In (a), 3 experienced tailors are half of the 6-tailor team and 5 trainees are half of the 10-trainee team. Two half-teams make one full team's worth of work, so the time is the same 15 days.

**Check the answer**

**(a)** has one trainee fewer than (a), so it should take a little longer than 15 days. $16\frac{2}{3}$ days fits.

**General lesson**

When workers have different rates, convert them into one common unit before using worker-days. Use the information "A or B can do the job in the same time" to find the exchange rate between them.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: A taller, longer wall
questions.stem: 6 artists paint a mural covering a wall 30 m long and 4 m high in 5 days. How many days will 8 artists take to paint a mural in the same style covering a wall 40 m long and 6 m high? All the artists work at the same steady rate, and both murals need the same amount of work for each square metre of wall.
hints: What measure of a wall decides how much painting it needs: its length, its height, or something built from both?

solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The wall changes in two directions at once. The amount of painting depends on the **area** of the wall, which is length × height. This is a hidden quantity that the question never names.

**Find the mathematical structure**

Days are proportional to the area to be painted and inversely proportional to the number of artists.

**Build the reasoning**

> 30 × 4 = 120 — *square metres in the first wall*\
> 40 × 6 = 240 — *square metres in the second wall*\
> 6 × 5 = 30 — *artist-days for 120 m²*\
> 30 ÷ 120 = $\frac{1}{4}$ — *artist-day for each square metre*\
> 240 × $\frac{1}{4}$ = 60 — *artist-days for the second wall*\
> 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 — *days*

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time**, starting from 5 days:

- area doubles (120 → 240 m²): multiply by 2;
- more artists (6 → 8): multiply by $\frac{6}{8}$ = $\frac{3}{4}$.

> 5 × 2 × $\frac{3}{4}$ = 7.5 — *days*

**Check the answer**

A common mistake is to scale by the length only (×$\frac{4}{3}$) or by the height only (×$\frac{3}{2}$). Using both gives $\frac{4}{3}$ × $\frac{3}{2}$ = 2, which is exactly the area factor. As a check: 8 artists for 7.5 days give 60 artist-days, and 240 m² at $\frac{1}{4}$ artist-day per square metre also needs 60 artist-days.

**General lesson**

Sometimes the quantity that matters is built from two others, such as area = length × height. Identify the real measure of the work before applying proportion.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Rice in the hostel
questions.stem: A hostel has enough rice to give 120 students 400 g each per day for 30 days. Before any rice is used, 30 more students arrive, and the daily ration is cut to 360 g per student.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: For how many complete days will the rice last?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How much rice is left after the last complete day?

hints: Work out the total amount of rice, then the amount used each day under the new arrangement.

solution.answer: **(a)** **26 complete days.** (b) **36 kg** left, which is not enough for a 27th day.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

The rice store is fixed. Daily use = (number of students) × (ration per student). Days = store ÷ daily use. Assumption: every student eats exactly the ration each day.

**Build the reasoning**

**The store:**

> 120 × 400 × 30 = 1,440,000 — *grams of rice*

That is 1,440 kg.

**New daily use:**

> 120 + 30 = 150 — *students*\
> 150 × 360 = 54,000 — *grams used each day, which is 54 kg*

**(a)**

> 1,440 ÷ 54 = $26\frac{2}{3}$ — *days' worth of rice*

So the rice lasts 26 complete days.

**(b)**

> 26 × 54 = 1,404 — *kilograms used in 26 days*\
> 1,440 − 1,404 = 36 — *kilograms left*

A 27th day would need 54 kg, so the 36 kg is not enough.

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time**, starting from 30 days:

- more students (120 → 150): multiply by $\frac{120}{150}$ = $\frac{4}{5}$;
- smaller ration (400 g → 360 g): multiply by $\frac{400}{360}$ = $\frac{10}{9}$.

> 30 × $\frac{4}{5}$ × $\frac{10}{9}$ = $26\frac{2}{3}$ — *days*

**Check the answer**

More students and a smaller ration pull in opposite directions. More students win: the rice now lasts under 27 days instead of 30.

**General lesson**

Compound proportion gives the exact number of days' worth of supply. When only complete days count, round down and report the leftover.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Wages for a team
questions.stem: 12 workers, each working 8 hours a day for 6 days, are paid ₹86,400 altogether. At the same rate of pay per hour, how much will 9 workers earn altogether for working 6 hours a day for 10 days?
hints: What is one worker paid for one hour?

solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Pay = (pay per worker-hour) × (worker-hours). Worker-hours = workers × hours per day × days.

**Build the reasoning**

> 12 × 8 × 6 = 576 — *worker-hours in the first job*\
> 86,400 ÷ 576 = 150 — *rupees per worker-hour*\
> 9 × 6 × 10 = 540 — *worker-hours in the second job*\
> 540 × 150 = 81,000 — *rupees*

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time**, starting from ₹86,400:

> 86,400 × $\frac{9}{12}$ × $\frac{6}{8}$ × $\frac{10}{6}$ = 81,000 — *rupees*

Fewer workers and shorter days lower the pay; more days raise it.

**Check the answer**

The second job has 540 worker-hours against 576, slightly fewer, so the pay should be slightly less than ₹86,400. It is.

**General lesson**

Combined units such as worker-hours work for money as well as for output: pay per worker-hour plays the role of a price per unit.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: A long road trip
questions.stem: Driving 6 hours a day at an average speed of 50 km/h, a family completes a long road trip in 8 days. How many days of driving would the same trip take if they drove 5 hours a day at an average speed of 64 km/h? (Count part of a day's driving as a fraction of a day.)
hints: What stays the same? Find it first.

solution.answer: **7.5 days** of driving: 7 full days, and then 2.5 hours of driving on the 8th day.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

The fixed quantity is the **distance** of the trip. Distance per day = speed × hours per day.

**Build the reasoning**

> 50 × 6 = 300 — *kilometres per day at first*\
> 300 × 8 = 2,400 — *kilometres in the trip*\
> 64 × 5 = 320 — *kilometres per day with the new plan*\
> 2,400 ÷ 320 = 7.5 — *days*

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time:** fewer hours per day (6 → 5) means more days, multiply by $\frac{6}{5}$; faster speed (50 → 64) means fewer days, multiply by $\frac{50}{64}$.

> 8 × $\frac{6}{5}$ × $\frac{50}{64}$ = 7.5 — *days*

**Check the answer**

The new plan covers 320 km a day instead of 300 km, a little more, so the trip should take a little less than 8 days. 7.5 days fits.

**General lesson**

Find the conserved total first (here, distance). Then each new plan is a rate per day, and the number of days is total ÷ daily rate.

questions.answer: **7.5 days** of driving: 7 full days, and then 2.5 hours of driving on the 8th day.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: More workers for the bridge
questions.stem: 40 workers can build a bridge in 60 days. After 20 days of work, 10 more workers join them. All the workers work at the same rate. How many days does the whole bridge take?
hints: Measure the bridge in worker-days. How much is done in the first 20 days?

solution.answer: **52 days** in total.
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

The job is fixed in worker-days. The story has two stages: 40 workers, then 50 workers. Times for stages done one after another add up.

**Build the reasoning**

> 40 × 60 = 2,400 — *worker-days for the bridge*\
> 40 × 20 = 800 — *worker-days done in the first 20 days*\
> 2,400 − 800 = 1,600 — *worker-days still to do*\
> 40 + 10 = 50 — *workers in the second stage*\
> 1,600 ÷ 50 = 32 — *days for the second stage*\
> 20 + 32 = 52 — *days in total*

**Alternative reasoning**

After 20 days, $\frac{1}{3}$ of the bridge is built, and the remaining $\frac{2}{3}$ would take the original 40 workers 40 more days. With 50 workers instead of 40, it takes $\frac{40}{50}$ of that time: $\frac{4}{5}$ × 40 = 32 days.

**Check the answer**

40 × 20 + 50 × 32 = 800 + 1,600 = 2,400 worker-days, the whole bridge.

**General lesson**

In staged problems, measure what is left at the moment conditions change, then apply proportion to that remainder.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Ploughing the fields
questions.stem: A farm's tractors, working 6 hours a day, plough all its fields in 18 days. For each change below, say whether the number of days goes up or down, and by what factor, when everything else stays the same.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Twice as many tractors.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Fields with 3 times the area.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Tractors working 9 hours a day instead of 6 hours a day.

parts.label: d
parts.stem: New tractors that each plough 1.5 times as fast as the old ones.

parts.label: e
parts.stem: If all four changes happen together, how many days are needed?

hints: For each change ask: does it make the job bigger, or the workforce stronger?

solution.answer: **(a)** Down: multiply by **$\frac{1}{2}$**. (b) Up: multiply by **3**. (c) Down: multiply by **$\frac{2}{3}$**. (d) Down: multiply by **$\frac{2}{3}$**. (e) **12 days.**
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

- The size of the job (area) is **directly** proportional to the days.
- The strength of the workforce (number of tractors, hours per day, speed of each tractor) is **inversely** proportional to the days.
- Each change multiplies the number of days by its own factor, so several changes multiply together.

**Build the reasoning**

- (a) Twice the tractors share the work: the time is halved, factor $\frac{1}{2}$.
- (b) Three times the area is three times the work: factor 3.
- (c) Hours per day go from 6 to 9, so each day does $\frac{9}{6}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$ as much: factor $\frac{6}{9}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$.
- (d) Each tractor does 1.5 = $\frac{3}{2}$ times as much: factor $\frac{2}{3}$.

> 18 × $\frac{1}{2}$ × 3 × $\frac{2}{3}$ × $\frac{2}{3}$ = 12 — *days*

**Develop intuition**

Combine the factors in pairs: twice the tractors with three times the work gives $\frac{3}{2}$ times the days; the longer days and faster tractors together divide the days by $\frac{3}{2}$ × $\frac{3}{2}$ = $\frac{9}{4}$. Overall, $\frac{3}{2}$ × $\frac{4}{9}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$, and $\frac{2}{3}$ of 18 days is 12 days.

**Check the answer**

The workforce becomes 2 × $\frac{3}{2}$ × $\frac{3}{2}$ = $\frac{9}{2}$ times as strong, while the job becomes 3 times as big. A stronger workforce on a job that grew less should finish sooner: 3 ÷ $\frac{9}{2}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$, so 12 days.

**General lesson**

In compound proportion, each change contributes its own factor and the factors multiply. Sort the quantities into "size of the job" (direct) and "strength of the workforce" (inverse).

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Feeding horses
questions.stem: Feeding 25 horses for 12 days costs ₹18,000. The price of the feed then rises by one fifth. What will it cost to feed 15 horses for 32 days at the new price? Every horse eats the same amount each day.
hints: What does it cost to feed one horse for one day at the old price? What does "rises by one fifth" do to that?

solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Cost = (cost per horse-day) × (horses) × (days). A price rise multiplies the cost per horse-day by 1 + $\frac{1}{5}$ = $\frac{6}{5}$.

**Build the reasoning**

> 25 × 12 = 300 — *horse-days at first*\
> 18,000 ÷ 300 = 60 — *rupees per horse-day at the old price*\
> 60 × $\frac{6}{5}$ = 72 — *rupees per horse-day at the new price*\
> 15 × 32 = 480 — *horse-days now*\
> 480 × 72 = 34,560 — *rupees*

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time**, starting from ₹18,000:

> 18,000 × $\frac{15}{25}$ × $\frac{32}{12}$ × $\frac{6}{5}$ = 34,560 — *rupees*

**Check the answer**

Without the price rise, 480 horse-days would cost 480 × 60 = ₹28,800; adding one fifth gives 28,800 + 5,760 = ₹34,560.

**General lesson**

A percentage or fractional change in a rate is just another factor. Find the cost of one combined unit (a horse-day), adjust it, then scale.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Packing gift boxes
questions.stem: 4 volunteers working for 5 hours pack 600 gift boxes. How many volunteers, packing at the same rate, are needed to pack 900 gift boxes in 3 hours?

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Solve it by changing one quantity at a time.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Solve it again using volunteer-hours.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Explain why the two methods must give the same answer.

hints: For (a): to pack more boxes in the same time, do you need more or fewer volunteers? To pack them in less time?

solution.answer: **10 volunteers**, by both methods. (c) Both methods use the same fact, that every volunteer-hour packs the same number of boxes, so they are the same calculation done in a different order.
solution.explanation:
**Build the reasoning**

**(a) One change at a time.** Start with 4 volunteers, 5 hours, 600 boxes.

- 900 boxes instead of 600, still in 5 hours: $\frac{900}{600}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$ times as many volunteers.

> 4 × $\frac{3}{2}$ = 6 — *volunteers to pack 900 boxes in 5 hours*

- 3 hours instead of 5: less time needs more volunteers, $\frac{5}{3}$ times as many.

> 6 × $\frac{5}{3}$ = 10 — *volunteers to pack 900 boxes in 3 hours*

**(b) Volunteer-hours.**

> 4 × 5 = 20 — *volunteer-hours for 600 boxes*\
> 600 ÷ 20 = 30 — *boxes per volunteer-hour*\
> 900 ÷ 30 = 30 — *volunteer-hours for 900 boxes*\
> 30 ÷ 3 = 10 — *volunteers working for 3 hours*

**Why they must agree**

Method (a) computes 4 × $\frac{900}{600}$ × $\frac{5}{3}$. Method (b) computes (900 ÷ (600 ÷ (4 × 5))) ÷ 3. Rearranging the second expression gives exactly the same multiplications and divisions. Both rest on a single assumption: each volunteer packs 30 boxes every hour, whoever they are and however many others are packing.

**Check the answer**

10 volunteers × 3 hours × 30 boxes = 900 boxes.

**General lesson**

"One at a time" and "combined units" are two views of the same structure. Use whichever is clearer, and use the other as a check.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: When the model breaks down
questions.stem: 5 painters paint 8 identical classrooms in 4 days.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Assuming every painter works at the same steady rate, how many painter-days does one classroom need?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: A teacher predicts that 10 painters would paint the 8 classrooms in 2 days. What assumptions make this prediction reasonable?

parts.label: c
parts.stem: She then predicts that 160 painters could finish all 8 classrooms in one hour of an 8-hour working day. Use the model to check her arithmetic, and then explain why the prediction is unrealistic.

hints: For (c), picture 20 painters squeezed into each classroom. What would actually happen?

solution.answer:
**(a)** **2.5 painter-days** per classroom.

**(b)** That every painter works equally fast, that painters do not get in each other's way, and that there is enough space, equipment and paint for everyone.

**(c)** The arithmetic is right: 20 painter-days is 160 painter-hours, and 160 painters supply 160 painter-hours in one hour. But the model has stopped matching reality: 20 painters in one room would be crowded, and wet paint needs time to dry between coats, however many painters there are.
solution.explanation:
**Build the reasoning**

**(a)**

> 5 × 4 = 20 — *painter-days for 8 classrooms*\
> 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 — *painter-days per classroom*

**(b)**

> 20 ÷ 10 = 2 — *days for 10 painters*

**(c)**

> 20 × 8 = 160 — *painter-hours for the 8 classrooms*\
> 160 ÷ 160 = 1 — *hour for 160 painters*

**Where the model breaks**

The inverse model "twice the workers, half the time" assumes that the work can be shared out perfectly. Real jobs have limits:

- **Space:** only a few people can work on one wall at a time.
- **Steps that must wait:** a second coat cannot start until the first coat is dry. Drying time does not shrink when more painters arrive, just as the shirts in problem 4.5 dried in the same time however many were on the line.
- **Organisation:** many workers need time to share out tasks and equipment.

So the model is reasonable for 10 painters, doubtful for 40, and clearly wrong for 160.

**General lesson**

Every proportional model has a range where it works. Always ask whether the assumptions still hold at the numbers you are using.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Seniors and juniors
questions.stem: On a building site, 2 senior workers do as much work in a day as 3 junior workers. A team of 4 seniors and 6 juniors finishes a job in 9 days. How many juniors must work alongside the 4 seniors so that the same job is finished in 6 days? All seniors work at the same rate as each other, and so do all juniors.
hints: Convert the seniors into junior-equivalents.

solution.answer: **12 juniors** (6 more than in the first team).
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Measure everyone in **junior-equivalents**. One senior = $\frac{3}{2}$ juniors. Then the job is a fixed number of junior-days.

**Build the reasoning**

> 4 × $\frac{3}{2}$ = 6 — *junior-equivalents from 4 seniors*\
> 6 + 6 = 12 — *junior-equivalents in the first team*\
> 12 × 9 = 108 — *junior-days in the job*\
> 108 ÷ 6 = 18 — *junior-equivalents needed to finish in 6 days*\
> 18 − 6 = 12 — *juniors to join the 4 seniors*

**Alternative reasoning**

**One change at a time.** To finish in 6 days instead of 9, the team must be $\frac{9}{6}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$ times as strong: 12 × $\frac{3}{2}$ = 18 junior-equivalents. The 4 seniors provide 6 of them, so 12 juniors are needed.

**Check the answer**

4 seniors and 12 juniors give 6 + 12 = 18 junior-equivalents, and 18 × 6 = 108 junior-days.

**General lesson**

Convert different workers into one unit before using inverse proportion. Then subtract the part of the workforce that is already fixed.

questions.answer: **12 juniors** (6 more than in the first team).

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: A hen and a half
questions.stem:
"A hen and a half lays an egg and a half in a day and a half. How many eggs do 6 hens lay in 6 days?"

Assume every hen lays at the same steady rate; the halves are just a way of describing that rate.

Many people answer 6 eggs. Find the correct answer and explain the error.
hints: Change one quantity at a time. What happens if you keep 1.5 hens but give them 6 days instead of 1.5 days?

solution.answer: **24 eggs.** The answer 6 changes the hens (×4) and the eggs (×4) together but forgets that the days also change (×4).
solution.explanation:
**Find the mathematical structure**

Eggs = (eggs per hen-day) × (hens) × (days). Both more hens and more days produce more eggs, so both factors multiply.

**Build the reasoning**

**One change at a time**, starting from 1.5 eggs:

- Hens 1.5 → 6: multiply the eggs by 4.

> 1.5 × 4 = 6 — *eggs from 6 hens in a day and a half*

- Days 1.5 → 6: multiply the eggs by 4 again.

> 6 × 4 = 24 — *eggs from 6 hens in 6 days*

**Through one hen-day:**

> 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25 — *hen-days in the given situation*\
> 1.5 ÷ 2.25 = $\frac{2}{3}$ — *of an egg per hen-day*\
> 6 × 6 × $\frac{2}{3}$ = 24 — *eggs*

**Develop intuition**

The answer 6 is the number of eggs that 6 hens lay in a day and a half. Leaving the hens for 6 days instead, four times as long, gives four times as many eggs.

**Check the answer**

At $\frac{2}{3}$ egg per hen-day, 1.5 hens in 1.5 days lay 2.25 × $\frac{2}{3}$ = 1.5 eggs, which matches the puzzle.

**General lesson**

In compound problems, track every quantity that changes. The puzzle's odd fractions are designed to distract from the simple fact that both the hens and the days were multiplied by 4.

questions.answer: **24 eggs.** The answer 6 changes the hens (×4) and the eggs (×4) together but forgets that the days also change (×4).

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Build a problem with answer 15
questions.stem:
Invent a compound-proportion problem about workers building a wall. It must contain the number of workers, the hours they work each day, the length of wall built and the number of days. In your problem:

- the number of workers is **doubled**,
- the hours worked per day are **halved**,
- the length of wall is multiplied by $\frac{3}{2}$, and
- the answer (the new number of days) is exactly **15 days**.

Solve your problem to show it works, and explain why the doubling and halving cancel each other.
hints: Work backwards: if only the length changed by $\frac{3}{2}$, what must the original number of days have been?

solution.answer: The original number of days must be **10**. One example: "6 workers, working 8 hours a day, build 120 m of wall in 10 days. How many days will 12 workers, working 4 hours a day, take to build 180 m of the same wall?" The answer is **15 days**.
solution.explanation:
**Designing the problem**

The new number of days = original days × (factor for workers) × (factor for hours) × (factor for length).

- Workers doubled: days × $\frac{1}{2}$.
- Hours halved: days × 2.
- Length × $\frac{3}{2}$: days × $\frac{3}{2}$.

> $\frac{1}{2}$ × 2 × $\frac{3}{2}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$ — *overall factor*

To get 15 days, the original must be 15 ÷ $\frac{3}{2}$ = 10 days. Any starting numbers of workers, hours and metres will do, as long as the original number of days is 10.

**Solving the example**

> 6 × 8 × 10 = 480 — *worker-hours to build 120 m*\
> 480 ÷ 120 = 4 — *worker-hours per metre*\
> 180 × 4 = 720 — *worker-hours to build 180 m*\
> 12 × 4 = 48 — *worker-hours per day in the new team*\
> 720 ÷ 48 = 15 — *days*

**Why doubling and halving cancel**

Twice as many workers each working half as many hours give the same number of worker-hours per day: 12 × 4 = 6 × 8 = 48. The team's daily effort does not change, so only the longer wall affects the answer.

**General lesson**

Designing a problem backwards from its answer shows how each factor works. Changes that leave the combined unit (worker-hours per day) unchanged have no effect on the answer.

questions.answer: The original number of days must be **10**. One example: "6 workers, working 8 hours a day, build 120 m of wall in 10 days. How many days will 12 workers, working 4 hours a day, take to build 180 m of the same wall?" The answer is **15 days**.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Upside-down factors
questions.stem:
18 workers, working 8 hours a day, dig a trench 240 m long in 10 days. A student finds how many days 12 workers, working 9 hours a day, need to dig a trench 180 m long:

"Days = 10 × $\frac{12}{18}$ × $\frac{9}{8}$ × $\frac{180}{240}$ = 5.625 days."

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Which of the student's factors are upside down? Explain how you can tell **without** calculating.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the correct number of days.

hints: For each change, ask: should it make the number of days bigger or smaller? Then check whether the student's factor is more than 1 or less than 1.

solution.answer:
**(a)** The **workers** factor and the **hours** factor are upside down. Fewer workers should mean **more** days, but $\frac{12}{18}$ is less than 1. Longer working days should mean **fewer** days, but $\frac{9}{8}$ is more than 1. The length factor $\frac{180}{240}$ is correct: a shorter trench needs fewer days.

**(b)** **10 days.**
solution.explanation:
**Build the reasoning**

**Correct factors:**

- Workers 18 → 12: more days, factor $\frac{18}{12}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$.
- Hours 8 → 9: fewer days, factor $\frac{8}{9}$.
- Length 240 → 180 m: fewer days, factor $\frac{180}{240}$ = $\frac{3}{4}$.

> 10 × $\frac{3}{2}$ × $\frac{8}{9}$ × $\frac{3}{4}$ = 10 — *days*

**Check with worker-hours:**

> 18 × 8 × 10 = 1,440 — *worker-hours for 240 m*\
> 1,440 ÷ 240 = 6 — *worker-hours per metre*\
> 180 × 6 = 1,080 — *worker-hours for 180 m*\
> 12 × 9 = 108 — *worker-hours per day in the new team*\
> 1,080 ÷ 108 = 10 — *days*

**Check the answer**

The changes pull in different directions: fewer workers (slower) but longer days and a shorter trench (faster). It is believable that they balance out exactly. The student's 5.625 days would mean that a smaller team finishes much faster, which should have raised suspicion.

**General lesson**

Write each factor only after deciding its direction. A factor that makes the answer bigger must be greater than 1, and one that makes it smaller must be less than 1.

fields.Section: Compound and mixed proportion

questions.title: Heaters at the research station
questions.stem: A polar research station has enough fuel to run 12 identical heaters, all day and every day, for 60 days. After 15 days, some extra heaters of the same kind are switched on, and from then on the remaining fuel lasts only 30 more days. Every heater burns fuel at the same steady rate. How many extra heaters were switched on?
hints: Measure the fuel in "heater-days": the fuel one heater burns in one day. How much is left after the first 15 days?

solution.answer: **6 extra heaters** were switched on, so 18 heaters were running after the change.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The story has two stages. For the first 15 days, 12 heaters burn fuel. Then more heaters are switched on, and the fuel that is left runs out after 30 more days. We must work backwards from "30 more days" to the number of heaters.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **What stays the same:** the amount of fuel, measured in **heater-days**. The amount at the start is fixed, and so is the amount left at the moment of the change.
- **What changes:** the number of heaters burning, and so how fast the fuel runs out.
- **Connection:** for the fuel left after the change, (number of heaters) × (days it lasts) = heater-days left.

**Build the reasoning**

**Step 1: the whole store.**

> 12 × 60 = 720 — *heater-days of fuel at the start*

**Step 2: what the first stage used.**

> 12 × 15 = 180 — *heater-days burned in the first 15 days*\
> 720 − 180 = 540 — *heater-days left at the change*

**Step 3: work backwards from 30 days.** The 540 heater-days are used up in 30 days, so each day must use:

> 540 ÷ 30 = 18 — *heater-days per day, so 18 heaters are running*\
> 18 − 12 = 6 — *extra heaters*

**Develop intuition**

Think of the fuel as 720 tickets, with every heater using one ticket a day. After 15 days, 540 tickets are left. If they are all gone after 30 more days, then 18 tickets were used each day: one for each of 18 heaters.

**Check the answer**

- 12 heaters for 15 days and 18 heaters for 30 days use 180 + 540 = 720 heater-days, the whole store.
- **Direction:** the fuel ran out sooner than planned (after 45 days instead of 60), so more heaters must have been running. 18 is more than 12.
- **Tempting error:** using the whole store again, 720 ÷ 30 = 24 heaters. That forgets the fuel already burned in the first 15 days.

**Alternative reasoning**

Without the change, the fuel left after 15 days would have lasted the 12 heaters 60 − 15 = 45 more days. It lasted only 30 days, which is $\frac{30}{45}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ as long. With a fixed amount of fuel, $\frac{2}{3}$ of the time means $\frac{3}{2}$ times as many heaters:

> 12 × $\frac{3}{2}$ = 18 — *heaters after the change*

**General lesson**

In a story with stages, stop the clock at the moment of change and measure what is left. Inverse proportion then works in either direction: from heaters to days, or, as here, backwards from days to heaters.

questions.answer: **6 extra heaters** were switched on, so 18 heaters were running after the change.

fields.Section: Olympiad modelling, changing conditions and hidden relationships

questions.title: Stops along the way
questions.stem: Whenever a bus is moving, it travels at 60 km/h. Because of its stops, its average speed for the whole journey is only 45 km/h.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: On average, for how many minutes is the bus stopped in each hour of the journey?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How long does a 270 km journey take?

parts.label: c
parts.stem: If the stops could be cut to 6 minutes in every hour, what would the average speed become?

hints: In one hour of the journey the bus covers 45 km. How long does it take to cover 45 km while it is moving?

solution.answer: **(a)** **15 minutes** in each hour. (b) **6 hours.** (c) **54 km/h.**
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

"Average speed 45 km/h" means that over the whole journey, stops included, the bus covers 45 km for every hour that passes. The moving speed tells us how much of each hour is spent actually moving.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Each hour of the journey splits into **moving time** and **stopped time**.
- Distance covered in an hour comes only from the moving time, at 60 km/h. That is 1 km for every minute of moving.
- **Hidden quantity:** the moving time in each hour. Once we know it, everything else follows.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)** In one hour of the journey the bus covers 45 km. At 1 km per minute of moving, that needs 45 minutes of moving.

> 45 ÷ 60 × 60 = 45 — *minutes of moving in each hour*\
> 60 − 45 = 15 — *minutes stopped in each hour*

**(b)** Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, so total time = total distance ÷ average speed.

> 270 ÷ 45 = 6 — *hours for the journey*

**(c)** With only 6 minutes of stops, the bus moves for 54 minutes of each hour, covering 54 km.

> 60 − 6 = 54 — *minutes of moving, so 54 km, in each hour*

**Develop intuition**

Picture each hour as a strip of 60 boxes, one for each minute. In 45 of the boxes the bus moves 1 km; in the other 15 it stands still. The average speed simply counts the kilometres in the strip.

**Check the answer**

- (b) In 6 hours the bus is stopped for 6 × 15 = 90 minutes, so it moves for 4.5 hours, and 4.5 × 60 = 270 km.
- The average speed must be less than the moving speed, because stops add time but no distance. Both 45 km/h and 54 km/h are less than 60 km/h.

**General lesson**

An average speed hides the stops inside it. Split the time into moving time and stopped time: the distance comes only from the moving time.

fields.Section: Olympiad modelling, changing conditions and hidden relationships

questions.title: Behind schedule in the tunnel
questions.stem: A company promises to dig a metro tunnel in 40 days, using 30 workers. All 30 workers dig every day, each at the same steady rate. After 25 days, only $\frac{2}{5}$ of the tunnel has been dug. How many more workers, digging at the same rate, must join so that the tunnel is finished on time?
hints: Do not trust the company's plan; trust what has actually happened. How many worker-days did $\frac{2}{5}$ of the tunnel take?

solution.answer: **45 more workers** must join, making 75 workers for the last 15 days.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The company planned 30 workers for 40 days, but after 25 days the tunnel is less than half dug. The plan was wrong about the size of the job. What has actually happened tells us the true size.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **What stays the same:** the amount of digging the tunnel really needs, measured in **worker-days**.
- **What the evidence says:** 30 workers for 25 days dug $\frac{2}{5}$ of the tunnel. That fixes the size of the whole job.
- **What remains:** $\frac{3}{5}$ of the tunnel, to be dug in the 40 − 25 = 15 days that are left.

**Build the reasoning**

**Step 1: the work already done.**

> 30 × 25 = 750 — *worker-days spent so far*

**Step 2: the true size of the job.** 750 worker-days dug two fifths, so one fifth needs half as much.

> 750 ÷ 2 = 375 — *worker-days for $\frac{1}{5}$ of the tunnel*\
> 5 × 375 = 1,875 — *worker-days for the whole tunnel*

**Step 3: what is left.**

> 3 × 375 = 1,125 — *worker-days for the remaining $\frac{3}{5}$*

**Step 4: workers needed in the last 15 days.**

> 1,125 ÷ 15 = 75 — *workers needed*\
> 75 − 30 = 45 — *extra workers*

**Check the answer**

- 30 workers for 25 days and 75 workers for 15 days give 750 + 1,125 = 1,875 worker-days, the whole tunnel.
- **Tempting error:** trusting the plan. The plan assumed 30 × 40 = 1,200 worker-days in all, leaving 1,200 − 750 = 450, so it seems that 450 ÷ 15 = 30 workers are enough and nobody extra is needed. But 750 worker-days produced only $\frac{2}{5}$ of the tunnel, so the plan was simply wrong.
- **Direction:** the $\frac{3}{5}$ still to dig is more than the $\frac{2}{5}$ already dug, and there is less time left (15 days instead of 25), so far more than 30 workers are needed.

**Alternative reasoning**

**Compare the two parts directly.** $\frac{2}{5}$ of the tunnel took 30 workers 25 days, so $\frac{1}{5}$ would take them 12.5 days, and the remaining $\frac{3}{5}$ would take them 3 × 12.5 = 37.5 days. To do it in 15 days instead, the team must be bigger by the factor:

> 37.5 ÷ 15 = 2.5 — *times as many workers*\
> 30 × 2.5 = 75 — *workers, as before*

**General lesson**

When the evidence contradicts a plan, believe the evidence. Use what has actually been achieved to measure the true size of a job, then plan the rest from there.

questions.answer: **45 more workers** must join, making 75 workers for the last 15 days.

fields.Section: Olympiad modelling, changing conditions and hidden relationships

questions.title: Volunteers who leave early
questions.stem: 24 volunteers, each working 8 hours a day, would finish clearing a park in exactly 20 days. Everyone works at the same steady rate. After 8 days of work, 8 of the volunteers leave.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How many hours a day must the remaining volunteers work to finish on time?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: The organisers decide that nobody should work more than 10 hours a day. If the remaining volunteers work 10 hours a day from day 9 onwards, on which day is the work finished, and how many working days later than planned is that?

hints: Measure the job in volunteer-hours. How many are left after the first 8 days?

solution.answer:
**(a)** **12 hours a day.**

**(b)** The 16 volunteers need 14.4 days instead of 12, so the work ends **4 hours into day 23** instead of at the end of day 20. It is **2.4 working days late** (2 days and 4 working hours).
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The plan would have worked, but a third of the team leaves after 8 days. The work that remains must now be shared by fewer people. They can make up for it by working longer each day, or by taking more days.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **What stays the same:** the work still to be done, measured in **volunteer-hours** (one volunteer working for one hour).
- Work supplied per day = (number of volunteers) × (hours per day).
- Days needed = work left ÷ work supplied per day.

**Build the reasoning**

**Step 1: the work left after 8 days.** The full team would have needed 20 − 8 = 12 more days.

> 24 × 8 × 12 = 2,304 — *volunteer-hours of work left*

**Step 2: the people who remain.**

> 24 − 8 = 16 — *volunteers*

**(a)** The 16 volunteers have 12 days to finish.

> 2,304 ÷ 12 = 192 — *volunteer-hours needed each day*\
> 192 ÷ 16 = 12 — *hours a day for each volunteer*

**(b)** At 10 hours a day, the team supplies:

> 16 × 10 = 160 — *volunteer-hours each day*\
> 2,304 ÷ 160 = 14.4 — *days needed*\
> 14.4 − 12 = 2.4 — *days late*

Counting from the start: days 9 to 22 are 14 full days, and 0.4 of a 10-hour day is 4 hours, so the work ends 4 hours into day 23.

**Develop intuition**

Losing a third of the team (8 of 24) means each remaining person must do $\frac{3}{2}$ times as much each day, and $\frac{3}{2}$ of 8 hours is 12 hours. Capping the day at 10 hours supplies only $\frac{10}{12}$ = $\frac{5}{6}$ of what is needed each day, so the remaining work takes $\frac{6}{5}$ times as long: $\frac{6}{5}$ of 12 days is 14.4 days.

**Check the answer**

- (a) 16 volunteers × 12 hours × 12 days: 192 × 12 = 2,304 volunteer-hours, the work that was left.
- (b) 14 full days supply 14 × 160 = 2,240 volunteer-hours, leaving 64, which the 16 volunteers finish in 64 ÷ 16 = 4 hours on day 23.

**Is 12 hours a day realistic?**

The calculation assumes every volunteer works as fast in the 12th hour as in the 1st. Real people tire, and very long days usually lower the work done per hour. A plan that needs 12-hour days for 12 days in a row is risky, which is probably why the organisers set a 10-hour limit. The model gives the arithmetic; judgement decides whether the arithmetic can be trusted.

**General lesson**

When a team shrinks part-way through, measure the work left in a combined unit such as volunteer-hours. Then any way of finishing (more hours per day, or more days) is a division of that fixed amount.

fields.Section: Olympiad modelling, changing conditions and hidden relationships

questions.title: Two readings of a tank
questions.stem: A tap fills a tank at a steady rate, and the tank was empty when the tap was turned on. At 10:00 a.m. the tank is $\frac{1}{4}$ full, and at 10:40 a.m. it is $\frac{2}{3}$ full.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: At what time will the tank be full?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: At what time was the tap turned on?

hints: What fraction of the tank fills in those 40 minutes? Twelfths make both fractions easy to compare.

solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

We are given two snapshots of the water level, and neither is at the start or at the end. We must find the rate from the change between the snapshots, then work forwards to "full" and backwards to "empty".

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **What stays the same:** the rate of filling, so equal fractions of the tank take equal times.
- **A convenient unit:** $\frac{1}{4}$ = $\frac{3}{12}$ and $\frac{2}{3}$ = $\frac{8}{12}$, so twelfths of the tank turn every amount into a whole number.

**Build the reasoning**

**Step 1: the change between the snapshots.**

> $\frac{2}{3}$ − $\frac{1}{4}$ = $\frac{5}{12}$ — *of the tank filled between 10:00 and 10:40*

**Step 2: the bridge of one twelfth.** Five twelfths took 40 minutes.

> 40 ÷ 5 = 8 — *minutes to fill $\frac{1}{12}$ of the tank*

**(a)** At 10:40 the tank still needs $\frac{1}{3}$ = $\frac{4}{12}$.

> 4 × 8 = 32 — *minutes after 10:40, which is 11:12 a.m.*

**(b)** At 10:00 the tank held $\frac{1}{4}$ = $\frac{3}{12}$, which took:

> 3 × 8 = 24 — *minutes, so the tap was turned on at 9:36 a.m.*

**Develop intuition**

Draw the tank as a column of 12 equal bands. Each band takes 8 minutes to fill. At 10:00, 3 bands are full; at 10:40, 8 bands are full. Counting bands forwards and backwards gives every time you need.

**Check the answer**

- From 9:36 a.m. to 11:12 a.m. is 96 minutes, and 12 bands at 8 minutes each also make 96 minutes.
- At 10:00, 24 minutes after the start, $\frac{24}{96}$ = $\frac{1}{4}$ of the tank is full, as stated.

**General lesson**

A steady rate can be found from any two snapshots: divide the change in amount by the change in time. Then you can run the clock forwards or backwards.

fields.Section: Olympiad modelling, changing conditions and hidden relationships

questions.title: Two pipes, two start times
questions.stem: Pipe A alone fills a tank in 12 hours, and pipe B alone fills it in 18 hours. Both pipes flow at steady rates, and the tank starts empty.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Pipe A is opened at 6:00 a.m. and pipe B at 8:00 a.m., and then both stay open. At what time is the tank full?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Pipe A is again opened at 6:00 a.m. The owner wants the tank to be full by 12 noon. By what time would pipe B have to be opened? Is that possible if neither pipe may be opened before 6:00 a.m.?

hints: Pretend the tank holds 36 buckets. How many buckets does each pipe pour in one hour?

solution.answer:
**(a)** **2:00 p.m.**

**(b)** B would have to be opened by **3:00 a.m.**, three hours **before** A. If neither pipe may be opened before 6:00 a.m., the plan is **impossible**: even with both pipes opened at 6:00 a.m., the tank is not full until 1:12 p.m.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The pipes do not start together. In (a), only A works for the first two hours, and after that both work. In (b) we know when the tank must be full and must work backwards to a starting time for B.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Pretend the tank holds 36 buckets, because 36 is the smallest number that both 12 and 18 divide. A pours 36 ÷ 12 = 3 buckets per hour and B pours 36 ÷ 18 = 2 buckets per hour.
- When both are open, their rates add: 5 buckets per hour.
- The water poured in each stage adds up to the whole tank.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)** From 6:00 to 8:00 only A is open.

> 2 × 3 = 6 — *buckets poured by 8:00 a.m.*\
> 36 − 6 = 30 — *buckets still needed*\
> 30 ÷ 5 = 6 — *hours with both pipes open*

Six hours after 8:00 a.m. is 2:00 p.m.

**(b)** From 6:00 a.m. to 12 noon, A pours for 6 hours.

> 6 × 3 = 18 — *buckets from A by noon*\
> 36 − 18 = 18 — *buckets that B must pour by noon*\
> 18 ÷ 2 = 9 — *hours that B must run before noon*

Nine hours before noon is 3:00 a.m.

**The best possible without breaking the rule** is to open both pipes at 6:00 a.m.:

> 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2 — *hours with both pipes open from the start*

7.2 hours is 7 hours 12 minutes, so the tank would be full at 1:12 p.m., which is after noon.

**Check the answer**

- (a) A runs 8 hours (6:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.) and pours 8 × 3 = 24 buckets; B runs 6 hours and pours 6 × 2 = 12 buckets. 24 + 12 = 36.
- (b) B from 3:00 a.m. pours 9 × 2 = 18 buckets and A pours 18 buckets by noon, 36 in all.

**Develop intuition**

Working backwards from a deadline can give an answer that breaks a rule of the story, here a start time earlier than the 6:00 a.m. rule allows. An impossible result like this is not a mistake in the arithmetic. It is the mathematics telling you that the plan cannot work.

**General lesson**

For pipes that start at different times, add up the water from each stage. When you work backwards from a deadline, check that the answer obeys every condition of the story.
