questions.title: The lamp post and the platform
questions.stem: A metro train moves at a steady speed. Its front passes a lamp post, and 10 seconds later its back passes the same lamp post. The same train crosses a 300 m platform completely in 25 seconds, from the moment its front reaches the start of the platform until its back leaves the far end. Find the train's speed, in kilometres per hour, and its length.
hints: In each case, how far does the front of the train travel? Compare the two distances and the two times.

solution.answer: The train travels at **72 km/h** (20 m/s) and is **200 m** long.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

We know neither the speed nor the length. Each observation on its own links them, but does not separate them. Putting the two observations together does.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Passing the post:** the front moves forward by exactly one train length. That takes 10 seconds.
- **Crossing the platform:** the front moves forward by one train length **plus** 300 m. That takes 25 seconds.
- **Hidden relationship:** the second movement is the first one with an extra 300 m added. So the extra 15 seconds are spent covering exactly the extra 300 m.

**Build the reasoning**

> 25 − 10 = 15 — *extra seconds, caused only by the 300 m platform*\
> 300 ÷ 15 = 20 — *metres per second*\
> 20 × 3.6 = 72 — *kilometres per hour*

In 10 seconds the train moves one length:

> 20 × 10 = 200 — *metres, the length of the train*

**Develop intuition**

Imagine a dot painted on the front of the train. To pass the post, the dot travels one train length. To cross the platform, the dot travels the whole platform and then one more train length, so that the back of the train can clear the end.

**Check the answer**

Crossing the platform, the front moves 200 + 300 = 500 m, and at 20 m/s that takes 500 ÷ 20 = 25 seconds, as stated.

**Why one observation is not enough**

"The back passes the post 10 seconds after the front" fits a 100 m train at 10 m/s, a 200 m train at 20 m/s, a 300 m train at 30 m/s, and so on. Only the second observation picks out one of these. When a problem has two unknowns, look for two separate facts about them.

**General lesson**

When two situations differ in only one way, the difference between their results is caused by that one change. Subtracting removes the unknown that both share, here the train's length.

questions.answer: The train travels at **72 km/h** (20 m/s) and is **200 m** long.

questions.title: Climb high, sleep low
questions.stem: Mountaineers set out from base camp to reach a summit 3,000 m higher. Every day they climb 600 m higher, and every evening they come back down 200 m to sleep at a lower, safer camp. (Real mountaineers often do this: "climb high, sleep low" helps the body get used to the thin air.) They leave base camp on the morning of day 1.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: On which day do they first reach the summit?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Sonia says: "They gain 400 m in each day and night, and 3,000 ÷ 400 = 7.5, so they reach the summit on day 8." Explain her mistake.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: On which day would they reach a summit 3,100 m above base camp?

hints: Make a table of their height each morning and the highest point they reach each day.

solution.answer:
**(a)** **Day 7.**

**(b)** Sonia makes them come back down 200 m after every day, including the last one. But on the day they reach the summit, they get there before that evening's descent, so the descent cannot stop them.

**(c)** **Day 8.**
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

Each 24 hours has two parts: a climb of 600 m and a descent of 200 m. The question is when they first **reach** the summit, and that happens during a day of climbing, before that evening's descent.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Each full day and night gives a net gain of 600 − 200 = 400 m.
- But the summit can be reached during the climbing part of a day. So the useful question is: "On which morning are they within 600 m of the summit?"
- Each morning they are 400 m higher than the morning before.

**Build the reasoning**

| Day | Height in the morning | Highest point that day |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 m | 600 m |
| 2 | 400 m | 1,000 m |
| 3 | 800 m | 1,400 m |
| 4 | 1,200 m | 1,800 m |
| 5 | 1,600 m | 2,200 m |
| 6 | 2,000 m | 2,600 m |
| 7 | 2,400 m | 3,000 m |

On the morning of day 7 they are at 2,400 m, and 3,000 − 2,400 = 600 m is exactly one day's climb. They reach the summit at the end of day 7.

**Without the table:** they reach the summit on the first day that starts within 600 m of the top.

> 3,000 − 600 = 2,400 — *metres they must reach by a morning*\
> 2,400 ÷ 400 = 6 — *full days and nights needed first*

So the summit is reached on day 6 + 1 = 7.

**(c)** For 3,100 m they must start a day at or above 3,100 − 600 = 2,500 m. Their morning heights go up in steps of 400 m: 2,400 m on day 7 is not enough, but 2,800 m on day 8 is. They reach the summit during day 8.

**Check the answer**

For 3,100 m: day 7 ends at 3,000 m, still 100 m short, so that evening they come back down to 2,800 m. On day 8 they climb from 2,800 m to 3,100 m after only 300 m of climbing.

**Why Sonia's method fails**

Sonia's method treats the climb as a steady rise of 400 m per day. That would be right if they lost height a little at a time all through the day. In fact they climb the full 600 m first and come down only in the evening. On the summit day the descent comes too late to matter, so the final stage is a full day's 600 m climb. When a process goes forward and then back, the last stage must be worked out separately.

**General lesson**

When progress goes "forward, then back", the target can be reached before the step back. Work out the last stage separately instead of dividing the whole distance by the net rate.

questions.title: Cars waiting for the ferry
questions.stem: 50 cars are waiting on one bank of a river to cross on a ferry that carries at most 8 cars at a time. Every crossing, in either direction, takes 10 minutes, including loading and unloading. The ferry starts on the cars' side, takes as many cars as it can on each trip, and comes straight back for more until every car is across.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long is it from the start of loading the first cars until the last car has been unloaded on the far bank?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How much time would be saved if the ferry could carry 10 cars at a time?

hints: Count crossings, not cars. How many crossings carry cars? How many empty trips back are there? Does the ferry need to come back after the last load?

solution.answer:
**(a)** **130 minutes** (2 hours 10 minutes): 7 crossings with cars and 6 empty crossings back.

**(b)** With 10 cars at a time it takes 90 minutes, a saving of **40 minutes**.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The time is not spent on each car but on each **crossing**. The ferry takes cars across and then comes back empty to fetch more, except after the very last load.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Hidden unit:** the crossing. Time = 10 minutes × (number of crossings).
- Loaded crossings: enough trips to carry 50 cars, 8 at a time. A part-full trip still takes a full crossing.
- Empty crossings: one fewer than the loaded crossings, because nobody needs the ferry to come back after the last car is across.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)**

> 50 ÷ 8 = 6.25 — *loads of cars*

Six trips carry only 48 cars, so a 7th trip is needed for the last 2 cars: 7 loaded crossings.

> 7 − 1 = 6 — *empty crossings back*\
> 7 + 6 = 13 — *crossings in all*\
> 13 × 10 = 130 — *minutes*

**(b)** With 10 cars per trip:

> 50 ÷ 10 = 5 — *loaded crossings*\
> 5 + 4 = 9 — *crossings, including 4 empty ones*\
> 9 × 10 = 90 — *minutes*\
> 130 − 90 = 40 — *minutes saved*

**Develop intuition**

Write the journey as a line of trips: load 1 across, back, load 2 across, back, and so on, ending with load 7 across. The loaded trips are like fence posts and the empty returns are like the gaps between them, so there is one fewer of them.

**Check the answer**

Three tempting wrong answers:

- 6.25 loads at 20 minutes per round trip gives 125 minutes, but the ferry cannot make a quarter of a trip.
- 7 round trips at 20 minutes each gives 140 minutes, but that counts a return after the last load that nobody needs.
- 50 ÷ 8 × 10 = 62.5 minutes forgets the empty returns altogether.

**General lesson**

Find what the time is really spent on. Here it is crossings, which come in whole numbers, and the final return is not needed. Count the pattern carefully, like posts and gaps.

questions.title: The shrinking cleaning team
questions.stem: A team of 10 cleaners, all working at the same steady rate, would need exactly 4 days to clean a stadium. They start together, but at the end of each day one cleaner leaves: 10 cleaners work on day 1, 9 on day 2, 8 on day 3, and so on.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: On which day is the cleaning finished?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: A smaller stadium needs exactly 4 days of work from 6 cleaners. A team of 6 starts it, and again one cleaner leaves at the end of each day. Is this cleaning ever finished? Explain.

hints: Measure each job in cleaner-days, then keep a running total of the work done, day by day.

solution.answer:
**(a)** It is finished at the end of **day 5**.

**(b)** **No.** The job needs 24 cleaner-days, but the shrinking team can supply only 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21 cleaner-days before nobody is left. $\frac{1}{8}$ of the job is never done.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The team gets smaller every day, so the work done each day keeps falling. We cannot divide the job by a fixed daily amount; we must add up the actual work, day by day.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Fixed:** the size of each job, in **cleaner-days**.
- **Changing:** the work done each day, which falls by one cleaner-day every day.
- The job is finished on the first day when the running total reaches the size of the job, if that ever happens.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)**

> 10 × 4 = 40 — *cleaner-days for the stadium*

| Day | Cleaners at work | Running total of work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 10 | 10 |
| 2 | 9 | 19 |
| 3 | 8 | 27 |
| 4 | 7 | 34 |
| 5 | 6 | 40 |

The total reaches exactly 40 at the end of day 5.

**(b)**

> 6 × 4 = 24 — *cleaner-days for the smaller stadium*\
> 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21 — *cleaner-days the shrinking team can ever supply*\
> 24 − 21 = 3 — *cleaner-days that are never done*\
> 3 ÷ 24 = $\frac{1}{8}$ — *of the job left undone*

After day 6 there are no cleaners left, so the job can never be finished.

**Check the answer**

**A tempting shortcut that fails.** "In (a) the team averages 8 cleaners, so it needs 40 ÷ 8 = 5 days." It happens to work, but only because the average over days 1 to 5 is exactly 8. Try the same shortcut on (b): the average of 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 cleaners is 3.5, and 24 ÷ 3.5 is about 6.9, which suggests the job is finished on day 7. But on day 7 there are no cleaners at all. The average hides the fact that the team runs out.

**Develop intuition**

Picture the work as a staircase of blocks: 10 blocks on day 1, 9 on day 2, and so on, each step one block lower. A staircase that gets lower every day has a largest possible number of blocks, and some jobs need more blocks than that.

**General lesson**

When the rate changes from stage to stage, add up the work stage by stage. Ask whether a job can be finished at all before asking when.

questions.title: Leaflets and minutes
questions.stem: A print shop uses the same machine for every order. An order of 200 leaflets takes 25 minutes, and an order of 500 leaflets takes 55 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Show that the time is not directly proportional to the number of leaflets.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find a simple model that fits both orders, and explain what each part of it could mean in the shop.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Use your model to predict how long an order of 800 leaflets takes.

parts.label: d
parts.stem: A customer predicts that 800 leaflets will take 4 × 25 = 100 minutes. Explain why this prediction is too long.

hints: How much extra time do the extra 300 leaflets take? Then see how much of the 25 minutes is left over.

solution.answer:
**(a)** If the time were proportional, 500 leaflets would take $\frac{500}{200}$ × 25 = 62.5 minutes, not 55.

**(b)** Time = **5 minutes of setting up** + **1 minute for every 10 leaflets**. The 5 minutes could be spent preparing the machine, loading the design and paper, and making a test print; after that the machine prints 10 leaflets per minute.

**(c)** **85 minutes.**

**(d)** The customer multiplies the 5 minutes of setting up by 4 as well, but setting up happens only once per order. That adds 15 minutes too many.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The two orders do not fit direct proportion. The data are telling us that part of the time does not grow with the number of leaflets.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Suppose the time has two parts: a **fixed** part that every order needs, and a part **proportional** to the number of leaflets.
- Comparing the two orders removes the fixed part, because each order includes it exactly once. The difference between them then gives the printing rate.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)**

> 25 ÷ 200 = 0.125 — *minutes per leaflet for the small order*\
> 55 ÷ 500 = 0.11 — *minutes per leaflet for the large order*

The time per leaflet is not the same, so the time is not directly proportional to the number of leaflets.

**(b)** Compare the two orders:

> 500 − 200 = 300 — *extra leaflets*\
> 55 − 25 = 30 — *extra minutes*\
> 300 ÷ 30 = 10 — *leaflets printed per minute*

At 10 leaflets per minute, printing 200 leaflets takes 20 minutes, so:

> 25 − 200 ÷ 10 = 5 — *minutes of fixed setting up*

**(c)**

> 5 + 800 ÷ 10 = 85 — *minutes for 800 leaflets*

**Check the answer**

The model gives 5 + 200 ÷ 10 = 25 minutes and 5 + 500 ÷ 10 = 55 minutes, matching both orders.

**An honest warning**

A fixed part plus a proportional part can always be made to fit **two** orders, so these two orders do not prove that the model is right. A third order would test it: the model predicts that 1,000 leaflets take 105 minutes. A good modeller says what the model assumes and how it could be checked.

**General lesson**

When data do not fit proportion, try "fixed part + proportional part". The difference between two cases removes the fixed part and reveals the rate. Then scale only the part that really grows.

questions.title: With and against the wind
questions.stem: Meena cycles from her house to the market with a steady wind behind her, and the trip takes 20 minutes. She cycles straight back along the same road against the same wind, and that takes 30 minutes. She pedals equally hard both ways, and the wind adds to her speed on the way there exactly as much as it takes away on the way back.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Can you work out the distance from her house to the market? Explain what you can and cannot work out from this information.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: You are now told that with no wind at all, Meena cycles at 15 km/h. Find the distance, and the amount by which the wind changes her speed.

hints: The road is the same both ways. What do the two times tell you about her two speeds?

solution.answer:
**(a)** **No**, the distance cannot be determined. We can find only comparisons: her speed with the wind is $\frac{3}{2}$ times her speed against it, the wind changes her speed by $\frac{1}{5}$ of her no-wind speed, and with no wind each trip would take 24 minutes.

**(b)** The distance is **6 km**, and the wind changes her speed by **3 km/h** (18 km/h with the wind, 12 km/h against it).
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

We know two times but no speed and no distance. Because the distance is the same both ways, the times can tell us how the two speeds compare, but not how big they are.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- For a fixed distance, speed and time are in **inverse proportion**. Times of 20 and 30 minutes mean the speeds are in the ratio 30 : 20 = 3 : 2.
- Call the speed with the wind 3 **parts** and the speed against it 2 parts. Her no-wind speed is exactly halfway between them, at 2.5 parts, and the wind's effect is 0.5 of a part.
- Nothing yet tells us how big one part is. That is the missing quantity.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)** Many different journeys fit the facts. For example:

| One part | With wind | Against wind | Distance (20 min with the wind) | Time back |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 km/h | 12 km/h | 8 km/h | 4 km | 30 min |
| 6 km/h | 18 km/h | 12 km/h | 6 km | 30 min |
| 8 km/h | 24 km/h | 16 km/h | 8 km | 30 min |

Every row matches both times but gives a different distance, so the distance cannot be determined. What every row shares is the ratio: the wind's effect (0.5 of a part) is always $\frac{1}{5}$ of the no-wind speed (2.5 parts). Every row also gives the same time for a trip with no wind, because the same distance is covered at 2.5 parts instead of 3:

> 20 × 3 ÷ 2.5 = 24 — *minutes each way with no wind*

**(b)** The no-wind speed is 2.5 parts, and it is 15 km/h.

> 15 ÷ 2.5 = 6 — *km/h in one part*\
> 3 × 6 = 18 — *km/h with the wind*\
> 2 × 6 = 12 — *km/h against the wind*\
> 18 − 15 = 3 — *km/h added or taken away by the wind*\
> 18 × $\frac{20}{60}$ = 6 — *kilometres to the market*

**Check the answer**

Going back at 12 km/h, 6 km takes $\frac{6}{12}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ hour, which is 30 minutes, as stated.

**General lesson**

Two times for the same distance give only the **ratio** of the speeds. To turn a ratio into actual speeds or distances, you need one actual measurement. Saying exactly what is missing is part of a complete answer.

questions.title: Three pairs of gardeners
questions.stem: Three gardeners each weed at their own steady rate. Asha and Bilal together can weed a large garden in 10 days. Bilal and Chetan together take 12 days, and Asha and Chetan together take 15 days.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long would all three take, working together?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How long would each of them take, working alone?

hints: Pretend the garden has 120 beds. How many beds does each pair weed in a day? What happens if you add the three pairs together?

solution.answer:
**(a)** **8 days.**

**(b)** Asha: **24 days**. Bilal: $17\frac{1}{7}$ **days** (about 17.14 days). Chetan: **40 days**.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

We are never told what one gardener does alone, only what pairs do. Each gardener belongs to exactly two of the three pairs. That is the hidden relationship to use.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Rates add for people working at the same time. If we add the three pairs, every gardener is counted **twice**, so we will have to halve.
- Pretend the garden has 120 beds. 120 is divisible by 10, 12 and 15, and it is twice their smallest common multiple, 60, so the rates stay whole numbers even after halving.

**Build the reasoning**

**The pairs' rates:**

> 120 ÷ 10 = 12 — *beds per day for Asha and Bilal*\
> 120 ÷ 12 = 10 — *beds per day for Bilal and Chetan*\
> 120 ÷ 15 = 8 — *beds per day for Asha and Chetan*

**Add the pairs.** This counts each gardener twice:

> 12 + 10 + 8 = 30 — *beds per day for two of each gardener*\
> 30 ÷ 2 = 15 — *beds per day for the three gardeners together*

**(a)**

> 120 ÷ 15 = 8 — *days for all three*

**(b)** Take a pair away from the team of three to find the person who is left.

> 15 − 10 = 5 — *beds per day for Asha (all three, minus Bilal and Chetan)*\
> 15 − 8 = 7 — *beds per day for Bilal*\
> 15 − 12 = 3 — *beds per day for Chetan*\
> 120 ÷ 5 = 24 — *days for Asha alone*\
> 120 ÷ 7 = $17\frac{1}{7}$ — *days for Bilal alone*\
> 120 ÷ 3 = 40 — *days for Chetan alone*

**Check the answer**

- Asha + Bilal = 5 + 7 = 12 beds per day; Bilal + Chetan = 7 + 3 = 10; Asha + Chetan = 5 + 3 = 8. All three pairs match.
- All three together (8 days) are faster than the fastest pair (10 days), as they must be.

**Alternative reasoning**

**With fractions of the garden.** The pairs weed $\frac{1}{10}$, $\frac{1}{12}$ and $\frac{1}{15}$ of the garden each day.

> $\frac{1}{10}$ + $\frac{1}{12}$ + $\frac{1}{15}$ = $\frac{1}{4}$ — *of the garden per day, for two of each gardener*\
> $\frac{1}{4}$ ÷ 2 = $\frac{1}{8}$ — *of the garden per day for all three, so 8 days*\
> $\frac{1}{8}$ − $\frac{1}{12}$ = $\frac{1}{24}$ — *of the garden per day for Asha (all three, minus Bilal and Chetan), so 24 days*

The 120-bed garden gives the same results while keeping every rate a whole number.

**General lesson**

When information comes in overlapping groups, add the groups and notice how many times each member has been counted. Then subtract to isolate each member.

fields.Section: Olympiad modelling, changing conditions and hidden relationships

questions.title: Hire now or hire later?
questions.stem:
A job needs exactly 600 worker-days of work (for example, 20 workers for 30 days), and it must be finished within 25 days. 20 workers are already on the job. The manager can hire extra workers, who work at the same rate as everyone else, in one of two ways:

- **Plan P:** 5 extra workers from day 1.
- **Plan Q:** 10 extra workers from day 11, after the first 10 days.

Everyone keeps working until the job is finished.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long does each plan take? Do both meet the deadline?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Every worker is paid the same amount for a day's work. Suppose workers are paid for exactly the time they work, so that a third of a day's work earns a third of a day's pay. Which plan costs less in wages?

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Explain your answer to (b) without calculating.

parts.label: d
parts.stem: Now suppose that anyone who works for any part of a day must be paid for the whole day. Which plan costs less now?

hints: For Plan Q, how much of the job is done in the first 10 days? For (b), what exactly does a wage bill pay for?

solution.answer:
**(a)** Plan P takes **24 days**; Plan Q takes $23\frac{1}{3}$ **days** (about 23.33 days). Both meet the deadline, and Plan Q finishes first.

**(b)** **Neither.** Both plans pay for exactly 600 worker-days.

**(c)** The job needs 600 worker-days however the work is scheduled, and the wages pay for exactly those worker-days.

**(d)** **Plan P**: it pays for 600 worker-days, while Plan Q pays for **620**.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

Two plans share out the same fixed job in different ways. We compare when they finish and what they cost.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Fixed:** the job, 600 worker-days.
- Plan P has one stage (25 workers). Plan Q has two stages (20 workers, then 30 workers).
- In (b), the wage bill matches the worker-days actually worked. In (d), any part of a day is paid as a whole day.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a) Plan P.**

> 600 ÷ 25 = 24 — *days with 25 workers*

**Plan Q.**

> 20 × 10 = 200 — *worker-days done in the first 10 days*\
> 600 − 200 = 400 — *worker-days left*\
> 400 ÷ 30 = $13\frac{1}{3}$ — *days with 30 workers*\
> 10 + $13\frac{1}{3}$ = $23\frac{1}{3}$ — *days in all*

Plan Q finishes $\frac{2}{3}$ of a day sooner, a third of the way through day 24.

**(b)** Plan P pays 25 workers for 24 days, which is 600 worker-days. Plan Q pays for 200 worker-days in its first stage and 30 × $13\frac{1}{3}$ = 400 worker-days in its second: 600 again.

**(d)** Plan P is unchanged, because it ends exactly at the end of day 24: 600 worker-days. In Plan Q the second stage runs into day 24, so its 30 workers are paid for 14 whole days:

> 200 + 30 × 14 = 620 — *worker-days paid in Plan Q*

**Why (b) needs no calculation**

Every worker-day of work is paid for once, and the job contains 600 worker-days of work whatever the plan. Hiring earlier or later changes **when** the work is done, not **how much** work there is. So if pay matches work exactly, every plan that finishes the job costs the same. Only an extra rule, such as paying for whole days, can make one plan more expensive than another.

**Check the answer**

- Plan Q: 200 + 400 = 600 worker-days, exactly the job.
- In (d), Plan Q pays each of its 30 workers for $\frac{2}{3}$ of a day that nobody works. That is 30 × $\frac{2}{3}$, which is 20 worker-days, exactly the difference between 620 and 600.

**General lesson**

A fixed amount of work costs a fixed amount of wages, however it is scheduled, as long as pay matches work exactly. Whole-number rules, such as paying for whole days, are what make the schedule matter.

questions.title: Sharing a taxi fairly
questions.stem:
Three friends share a taxi from the station. The fare is ₹30 for every kilometre the taxi travels, with no fixed charge. Ira gets out after 10 km, Jai after 20 km, and Kiran rides the whole 30 km, so the meter shows ₹900 at the end.

Kiran suggests: "Let's pay in proportion to the distance each of us rode, 10 : 20 : 30."

Ira suggests: "Let's split the cost of each stretch of the ride equally among the people who were in the taxi during that stretch."

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Work out what each friend pays under each suggestion, and check that each suggestion collects exactly ₹900.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Which suggestion do you think is fairer? Give a reason based on what each friend actually used.

hints: Split the ride into three 10 km stretches. Who is in the taxi during each stretch, and what does each stretch cost?

solution.answer:
**(a)** Each friend pays:

| Friend | Kiran's suggestion | Ira's suggestion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ira | ₹150 | ₹100 |
| Jai | ₹300 | ₹250 |
| Kiran | ₹450 | ₹550 |
| Total | ₹900 | ₹900 |

**(a)** Many people find **Ira's suggestion fairer**, because the meter charges for kilometres travelled by the taxi, not for each passenger. While three people share the taxi they share its cost, and for the last 10 km Kiran has the taxi to himself, so he pays for all of that stretch. A clearly argued case for Kiran's suggestion (it is simpler, and everyone pays the same amount for each kilometre ridden) is also a reasonable answer.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The fare depends only on how far the taxi travels. Three people use the taxi for different distances, and they must share one bill. The question does not give a rule for sharing, so part of the task is to judge which model matches the situation.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Kiran's model:** share the cost in proportion to **person-kilometres** (one person riding one kilometre). Everyone pays the same price per kilometre ridden.
- **Ira's model:** share the cost stretch by stretch. The cost of each stretch is split among the people in the taxi at the time.
- Both models collect the whole fare. They differ in what they treat as the thing being paid for.

**Build the reasoning**

**Kiran's suggestion.** Together the friends ride 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 person-kilometres.

> 900 ÷ 60 = 15 — *rupees per person-kilometre*\
> 10 × 15 = 150 — *rupees for Ira*\
> 20 × 15 = 300 — *rupees for Jai*\
> 30 × 15 = 450 — *rupees for Kiran*

**Ira's suggestion.** Each 10 km stretch costs 10 × ₹30 = ₹300.

> 300 ÷ 3 = 100 — *rupees each for the first stretch (all three in the taxi)*\
> 300 ÷ 2 = 150 — *rupees each for the second stretch (Jai and Kiran)*

So Ira pays ₹100, Jai pays 100 + 150 = ₹250, and Kiran pays 100 + 150 + 300 = ₹550, because he rides the last stretch alone.

> 100 + 250 + 550 = 900 — *rupees collected*

**Weighing the two models**

- Under Kiran's plan, Kiran pays only ₹450 for a ride that would cost ₹900 on his own. For the last 10 km he is the only passenger, yet the other two help to pay for a stretch they were not even in the taxi for.
- Under Ira's plan, each person pays only for stretches when they were in the taxi, and shares each stretch with whoever was there.
- Under **both** plans, everyone pays less than a taxi of their own would cost (₹300 for Ira, ₹600 for Jai, ₹900 for Kiran), so sharing helps everybody either way.

Notice that each friend suggested the plan that charges them less. Mathematics cannot decide what is "fair", but it can show exactly what each rule charges for, so the argument can be about the rule instead of the arithmetic.

**General lesson**

Before sharing a cost, decide what the cost is really for, here kilometres travelled by the taxi. Different models of the same situation can all add up correctly yet share the cost differently, so the choice of model matters.

questions.title: The clock that runs fast
questions.stem: A wall clock runs fast: whenever 60 real minutes pass, its hands move as if 63 minutes had passed. It is set to the correct time at 8:00 a.m.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: That afternoon, the clock shows 3:00. What is the correct time?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Ravi answers (a) like this: "From 8:00 to 3:00 is 7 hours, so the clock has gained 7 × 3 = 21 minutes, and the correct time is 2:39 p.m." Explain why Ravi is slightly wrong.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: If nobody adjusts the clock, when will it next show exactly the correct time? (Its face does not show a.m. or p.m.)

hints: Ravi's 7 hours are hours on the clock, not real hours. How many real minutes match 63 clock-minutes?

solution.answer:
**(a)** **2:40 p.m.**

**(b)** Ravi assumes that 7 **real** hours have passed. In fact the clock's 7 hours took only 6 hours 40 minutes of real time, and in that time the clock gains 20 minutes, not 21.

**(c)** At **8:00 a.m., exactly 10 days later**, when the clock has gained a full 12 hours.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

There are two kinds of minutes here: **real minutes** and **clock-minutes** (the amount the hands move). The clock squeezes 63 clock-minutes into every 60 real minutes. The clock's reading tells us how many clock-minutes have passed, but we want the real time.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Constant:** the exchange rate between the two kinds of minutes, 63 clock-minutes for every 60 real minutes.
- So clock-minutes and real minutes are in direct proportion, but we must cross the bridge in the right direction: from clock-minutes to real minutes.

**Build the reasoning**

**(a)** From 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. on the clock is 7 clock-hours.

> 7 × 60 = 420 — *clock-minutes shown*\
> 420 ÷ 63 = $\frac{20}{3}$ — *lots of 63 clock-minutes*\
> $\frac{20}{3}$ × 60 = 400 — *real minutes that have passed*

400 real minutes is 6 hours 40 minutes, and 6 hours 40 minutes after 8:00 a.m. is 2:40 p.m.

**(b)** In 6 hours 40 minutes, which is $\frac{20}{3}$ real hours, the clock gains 3 minutes in each real hour:

> $\frac{20}{3}$ × 3 = 20 — *minutes gained*

Adding 20 minutes to 2:40 p.m. gives 3:00 p.m., which matches the clock. Ravi's 21 minutes would be right only if 7 real hours had passed.

**(c)** A 12-hour clock face looks correct again once the clock has gained exactly 12 hours.

> 12 × 60 = 720 — *minutes the clock must gain*\
> 720 ÷ 3 = 240 — *real hours needed*\
> 240 ÷ 24 = 10 — *days*

After exactly 10 days the real time is 8:00 a.m. again. The clock is then exactly 12 hours ahead, so its hands also point to 8:00.

**Develop intuition**

Think of the clock as a runner who is a little faster than real time. Ravi measures the race by how far the runner went, which is slightly too far. For the real time, we must ask how long the runner took.

**Check the answer**

- **Direction:** the clock runs fast, so the correct time must be **earlier** than 3:00 p.m. 2:40 p.m. is earlier.
- **Size:** the clock gains about 3 minutes in each of about 7 hours, so the error should be about 20 minutes. It is exactly 20.

**General lesson**

When two clocks, scales or units disagree, write down the exchange rate between them and convert in the right direction. Here "3 minutes per hour" means per **real** hour, because that is how the rate was defined.

questions.title: One pipe, then the other
questions.stem: With pipes A and B both open, an empty tank fills in 12 minutes. One day the tank is empty again, and pipe A is opened on its own for 8 minutes and then closed. Pipe B is then opened on its own, and the tank becomes full after B has run for 18 minutes. Each pipe always flows at its own steady rate. How long would each pipe take to fill the empty tank on its own?
hints: Can you rewrite "A for 8 minutes, then B for 18 minutes" as "both together for some minutes, then B alone for the rest"?

solution.answer: Pipe A alone takes **20 minutes**, and pipe B alone takes **30 minutes**.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

We know what the two pipes do together, and what a mixture of A on its own and B on its own does. We need each pipe's own rate.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- The order in which the pipes run does not change how much water they deliver. So "A for 8 minutes, then B for 18 minutes" delivers the same water as "A and B together for 8 minutes, then B alone for 10 more minutes".
- We know exactly what 8 minutes together delivers, because together the pipes fill the tank in 12 minutes.

**Build the reasoning**

**Step 1: regroup the running times.** Split B's 18 minutes into 8 + 10, and pair 8 minutes of B with the 8 minutes of A.

> 18 − 8 = 10 — *minutes of B left over after pairing*

**Step 2: what the paired minutes delivered.** Together, the pipes fill $\frac{1}{12}$ of the tank each minute.

> 8 × $\frac{1}{12}$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ — *of the tank from the 8 paired minutes*

**Step 3: what B's extra 10 minutes delivered.**

> 1 − $\frac{2}{3}$ = $\frac{1}{3}$ — *of the tank from B alone in 10 minutes*\
> 10 × 3 = 30 — *minutes for B to fill the whole tank alone*

**Step 4: pipe A.** A's rate is the combined rate minus B's rate.

> $\frac{1}{12}$ − $\frac{1}{30}$ = $\frac{1}{20}$ — *of the tank per minute from A*

So A alone takes 20 minutes.

**Check the answer**

- A for 8 minutes fills $\frac{8}{20}$ = $\frac{2}{5}$ of the tank, and B for 18 minutes fills $\frac{18}{30}$ = $\frac{3}{5}$. Together, $\frac{2}{5}$ + $\frac{3}{5}$ = 1 whole tank.
- Together the pipes fill $\frac{1}{20}$ + $\frac{1}{30}$ = $\frac{3}{60}$ + $\frac{2}{60}$ = $\frac{5}{60}$ = $\frac{1}{12}$ of the tank per minute, so 12 minutes, as given.

**Alternative reasoning**

**A convenient tank size.** Pretend the tank holds 60 buckets, so together the pipes pour 60 ÷ 12 = 5 buckets per minute. If A pours some number of buckets per minute, B pours the rest of the 5. Testing whole numbers: if A pours 3 buckets per minute, then B pours 2, and 8 minutes of A plus 18 minutes of B give 24 + 36 = 60 buckets, exactly a full tank. So A takes 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes and B takes 60 ÷ 2 = 30 minutes. The regrouping method finds this without any guessing.

**General lesson**

Amounts of work done at different times can be regrouped. Pair up equal times of A and B to use what you know about them together; the leftover time shows one agent on its own.

questions.answer: Pipe A alone takes **20 minutes**, and pipe B alone takes **30 minutes**.

questions.title: How full was the tank?
questions.stem:
A tank is partly full of water. Three separate experiments are carried out, each starting from this same level:

- With only inlet pipe A open, the tank becomes full in 3 hours.
- With only drain B open, the tank becomes empty in 2 hours.
- With both A and B open, the tank becomes empty in 6 hours.

A and B always work at their own steady rates.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: What fraction of the tank was full at the start?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: How long would pipe A take to fill the tank from empty, and how long would drain B take to empty a full tank?

hints: Compare the second and third experiments. In 6 hours, how much water would B remove on its own? So how much must A have added in those 6 hours?

solution.answer:
**(a)** The tank was **half full** ($\frac{1}{2}$).

**(b)** A fills an empty tank in **6 hours**, and B empties a full tank in **4 hours**.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

No amount of water is given, only times. We must find the starting amount from the way the three experiments are related.

**Find the mathematical structure**

Call the water in the tank at the start **one load**. We measure everything in loads first, and connect loads to the whole tank at the end.

- B removes one load in 2 hours.
- A, in 3 hours, fills exactly the empty space above the starting level.
- A and B together remove one load in 6 hours.

**Build the reasoning**

**Step 1: what B does in 6 hours.** B removes one load every 2 hours.

> 6 ÷ 2 = 3 — *loads that B removes in 6 hours*

**Step 2: what A adds in those 6 hours.** With both open, only one load disappears in 6 hours, so A must have put back the other two.

> 3 − 1 = 2 — *loads added by A in 6 hours*\
> 2 ÷ 6 × 3 = 1 — *load added by A in 3 hours*

**Step 3: connect loads to the tank.** In the first experiment A, in 3 hours, fills the empty space above the starting level. We have just found that A adds one load in 3 hours. So the empty space is also one load: the water and the empty space are equal.

> 1 + 1 = 2 — *loads in the full tank, so the tank started half full*

**(b)** A adds one load, which is half the tank, in 3 hours.

> 2 × 3 = 6 — *hours for A to fill an empty tank*

B removes half the tank in 2 hours.

> 2 × 2 = 4 — *hours for B to empty a full tank*

**Check the answer**

In fractions of the tank, A adds $\frac{1}{6}$ per hour and B removes $\frac{1}{4}$ per hour.

- A alone from half full: $\frac{1}{2}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{6}$ = 3 hours to fill the tank.
- B alone from half full: $\frac{1}{2}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{4}$ = 2 hours to empty it.
- Both together: the level falls by $\frac{1}{4}$ − $\frac{1}{6}$ = $\frac{1}{12}$ of the tank each hour, so half a tank empties in $\frac{1}{2}$ ÷ $\frac{1}{12}$ = 6 hours.

All three experiments match.

**Develop intuition**

The key step is choosing the unit. Measuring in "loads" (the starting water) instead of "tanks" makes the second and third clues simple, and comparing them shows what A does by itself.

**General lesson**

When no amount is given, choose a convenient unknown amount as your unit, express every clue in that unit, and let the clues reveal how it compares with the whole.

questions.title: Two candles
questions.stem: Two new candles have the same length but different thicknesses. The thin one would burn away completely in 3 hours, and the thick one in 4 hours, each getting shorter at its own steady rate. They are lit at the same moment.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: After how long is the thick candle exactly twice as long as the thin one?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: The length of the candles is not given. Does that matter? Explain.

hints: Choose a convenient length, such as 12 cm. How many centimetres does each candle lose per hour? Then try a different length.

solution.answer:
**(a)** After $2\frac{2}{5}$ hours (2.4 hours), which is **2 hours 24 minutes**.

**(b)** **No.** Each hour, each candle loses the same fraction of its **starting** length ($\frac{1}{3}$ for the thin one, $\frac{1}{4}$ for the thick one), so at any moment the two remaining lengths are fixed fractions of the same starting length. When we compare them, the starting length cancels out, so any length gives the same answer.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The thin candle burns away faster. At the start the candles are equal; after 3 hours the thin one is gone while a quarter of the thick one is left. Somewhere in between, the thick candle must be exactly twice as long as the thin one.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- Each candle shrinks at a steady rate, so the length **burned** is proportional to the time. The length **remaining** is not proportional to the time: it is the starting length minus the length burned.
- Choose a length that makes both rates whole numbers: 12 cm, because 12 is divisible by both 3 and 4.

**Build the reasoning**

With 12 cm candles, the thin candle loses 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm per hour and the thick candle loses 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cm per hour.

| Time | Thin candle | Thick candle | Thick ÷ thin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 h | 12 cm | 12 cm | 1 |
| 1 h | 8 cm | 9 cm | $\frac{9}{8}$ |
| 2 h | 4 cm | 6 cm | $\frac{3}{2}$ |
| 3 h | 0 cm | 3 cm | the thin one is gone |

The answer lies between 2 and 3 hours. At 2 hours the thick candle (6 cm) is 2 cm short of twice the thin one (2 × 4 = 8 cm). After that, each hour the thick candle loses 3 cm, while "twice the thin candle" loses 2 × 4 = 8 cm. So the 2 cm shortfall closes by 8 − 3 = 5 cm per hour.

> 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4 — *hours after the 2-hour mark*\
> 2 + 0.4 = 2.4 — *hours, which is 2 hours 24 minutes*

**Check the answer**

At 2.4 hours the thin candle is 12 − 4 × 2.4 = 2.4 cm long and the thick candle is 12 − 3 × 2.4 = 4.8 cm long, and 4.8 is exactly twice 2.4.

**Why the length does not matter**

Try 24 cm candles instead. Every length in the table doubles: the thin candle loses 8 cm per hour and the thick one 6 cm per hour. At 2.4 hours they are 4.8 cm and 9.6 cm long, and 9.6 is still exactly twice 4.8. Doubling, tripling or halving the starting length multiplies **both** remaining lengths by the same number, so the comparison between them does not change.

In general, after any time the thin candle has the fraction 1 − (time ÷ 3) of its length left, and the thick one has 1 − (time ÷ 4) of the same length left. The question compares these two fractions, so the actual length plays no part.

**General lesson**

A quantity that seems to be missing may cancel out. Test this by trying one convenient value and then another. If the answer does not change, the quantity was never needed, and you can often explain why.

questions.title: Eight loaves, eight coins
questions.stem:
Two travellers stop for a meal. Arun has 5 loaves of bread and Bela has 3 loaves, all the same size. A hungry stranger asks to join them. The three of them share all 8 loaves equally, and the stranger then pays 8 coins for the bread he ate.

Arun says, "I brought 5 loaves and you brought 3, so I get 5 coins and you get 3."

How should the 8 coins be shared, so that each traveller is paid for the bread that he or she gave to the stranger? Is Arun's split fair?
hints: How much bread does each person eat? So how much of their own bread does each traveller give to the stranger?

solution.answer: Arun should get **7 coins** and Bela **1 coin**. Arun's 5 : 3 split is **not** fair: it pays the travellers in proportion to the bread they brought, including the bread they ate themselves. Surprisingly, it is unfair to Arun himself.
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

The stranger pays only for the bread **he** ate, not for all 8 loaves. Arun and Bela also ate some of their own bread. Each traveller should be paid only for the part of their bread that went to the stranger.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **Constant:** the price the stranger pays for each loaf he ate.
- **Hidden quantity:** how much bread each traveller gave to the stranger, which is their own loaves minus what they ate themselves.
- Payment is directly proportional to the bread **given**, not to the bread **brought**.

**Build the reasoning**

**Step 1: everyone's share.**

> 8 ÷ 3 = $\frac{8}{3}$ — *loaves eaten by each person, which is $2\frac{2}{3}$ loaves*

**Step 2: what each traveller gave.**

> 5 − $\frac{8}{3}$ = $\frac{7}{3}$ — *loaves Arun gave to the stranger*\
> 3 − $\frac{8}{3}$ = $\frac{1}{3}$ — *loaf Bela gave to the stranger*\
> $\frac{7}{3}$ + $\frac{1}{3}$ = $\frac{8}{3}$ — *loaves, exactly what the stranger ate*

**Step 3: the price of a loaf.**

> 8 ÷ $\frac{8}{3}$ = 3 — *coins for each loaf the stranger ate*

**Step 4: payment.**

> $\frac{7}{3}$ × 3 = 7 — *coins for Arun*\
> $\frac{1}{3}$ × 3 = 1 — *coin for Bela*

**Develop intuition**

Cut every loaf into thirds. There are 24 thirds, and each person eats 8 of them. Arun brought 15 thirds, ate 8 and gave 7 to the stranger. Bela brought 9 thirds, ate 8 and gave only 1. The stranger's 8 thirds came 7 from Arun and 1 from Bela, so the coins split 7 and 1.

**Check the answer**

- 7 + 1 = 8 coins, all paid out.
- Under Arun's split, Bela would receive 3 coins, the price of a whole loaf, although she gave the stranger only a third of a loaf. Arun would receive 5 coins for the $2\frac{1}{3}$ loaves he gave, when they are worth 7 coins.

**General lesson**

In fair-sharing problems, find exactly what each person contributed to the thing being paid for. Here it is the bread given away, not the bread brought, and that changes 5 : 3 into 7 : 1.

questions.answer: Arun should get **7 coins** and Bela **1 coin**. Arun's 5 : 3 split is **not** fair: it pays the travellers in proportion to the bread they brought, including the bread they ate themselves. Surprisingly, it is unfair to Arun himself.

questions.title: After they meet
questions.stem: Asha sets off from town P towards town Q, and at the same moment Bilal sets off from Q towards P along the same road. Each walks at a steady speed. They meet, pass each other and carry on. After the meeting, Asha takes 4 more hours to reach Q, and Bilal takes 9 more hours to reach P.

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long after setting off did they meet?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Who walks faster, and how many times as fast?

hints: Call the meeting point M. Asha walks from M to Q in 4 hours, but Bilal walked that same stretch before the meeting. How long did that take him?

solution.answer:
**(a)** They met **6 hours** after setting off.

**(b)** **Asha** walks faster, $\frac{3}{2}$ times as fast as Bilal (1.5 times as fast).
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

Neither a speed nor a distance is given, only times. The hidden relationship is that each stretch of road is walked by **both** people, at different speeds.

**Find the mathematical structure**

Call the meeting point M, and call the time from setting off until the meeting the **meeting time**.

- **Stretch MQ:** Bilal walked it before the meeting, taking the meeting time. Asha walks it after the meeting, taking 4 hours.
- **Stretch PM:** Asha walked it before the meeting, taking the meeting time. Bilal walks it after the meeting, taking 9 hours.
- On the same stretch, speed and time are in inverse proportion, so each stretch tells us how Asha's speed compares with Bilal's.

**Build the reasoning**

**From stretch MQ:** Asha needs 4 hours where Bilal needs the meeting time, so Asha's speed ÷ Bilal's speed = (meeting time) ÷ 4.

**From stretch PM:** Asha needs the meeting time where Bilal needs 9 hours, so Asha's speed ÷ Bilal's speed = 9 ÷ (meeting time).

Both describe the same comparison, so (meeting time) ÷ 4 = 9 ÷ (meeting time). Multiplying both sides by 4 and by the meeting time gives: (meeting time) × (meeting time) = 4 × 9 = 36.

> 6 × 6 = 36 — *so the meeting time is 6 hours*

**(b)**

> 6 ÷ 4 = $\frac{3}{2}$ — *Asha's speed compared with Bilal's*

As a check, the other stretch gives 9 ÷ 6, which is also $\frac{3}{2}$.

**Check the answer**

Try actual speeds: Bilal at 2 km/h and Asha at 3 km/h. In 6 hours Asha walks 18 km and Bilal 12 km, so the road is 30 km long and M is 18 km from P. After the meeting, Asha has 12 km left at 3 km/h, which takes 4 hours. Bilal has 18 km left at 2 km/h, which takes 9 hours. Both match.

**Develop intuition**

The meeting time sits "in the middle" of 4 hours and 9 hours in a multiplying sense: 4 is to 6 as 6 is to 9, since each step multiplies by $\frac{3}{2}$. To find such a middle number, ask which number multiplied by itself gives 4 × 9.

**General lesson**

When the same distance is covered by two people, the ratio of their times is the ratio of their speeds turned upside down. Writing the same ratio in two different ways is a powerful way to create an equation.

questions.title: Meeting twice on the road
questions.stem: Two walkers start at the same moment from the two ends, A and B, of a straight road 12 km long, and walk towards each other, each at a steady speed. They first meet 5 km from A. Each walker carries on to the far end of the road, turns round immediately, and walks back. Where do they meet for the second time?
hints: At the first meeting, how many road-lengths have the two walkers covered between them? How many have they covered by the second meeting?

solution.answer: They meet for the second time **3 km from B** (that is, 9 km from A).
solution.explanation:
**Understand the situation**

Neither speed is given, and the second meeting happens after both walkers have turned round. It looks as though we need the speeds. The key is to measure distances in road-lengths.

**Find the mathematical structure**

- **First meeting:** together the walkers have covered exactly **one** road-length (12 km), and the walker from A has covered 5 km of it.
- **Second meeting:** each walker has reached the far end (two road-lengths between them) and then they have walked towards each other until they meet (one more road-length between them). Together they have covered **three** road-lengths.
- Their speeds are steady, so the distance each walker covers is proportional to the time. Three times the combined distance means three times the time, so each walker has walked three times their first-meeting distance.

**Build the reasoning**

> 3 × 12 = 36 — *kilometres covered by the two walkers together by the second meeting*\
> 3 × 5 = 15 — *kilometres walked by the walker from A*

The walker from A walks 12 km to B, then 15 − 12 = 3 km back towards A. So the second meeting is 3 km from B.

**Check the answer**

**Try actual speeds** that fit the first meeting, such as 5 km/h for the walker from A and 7 km/h for the walker from B. Together they close the 12 km gap in 12 ÷ 12 = 1 hour, meeting 5 km from A. The walker from B reaches A after $\frac{12}{7}$ hours (about 1.7 hours) and turns; the walker from A reaches B after $\frac{12}{5}$ hours (2.4 hours) and turns. Together they walk 12 km each hour, so they have covered 36 km after 3 hours. By then the walker from A has gone 15 km (3 km back from B) and the walker from B has gone 21 km (9 km back from A). Both are at the same point, 3 km from B.

**When does the "three road-lengths" idea work?**

The argument needs both walkers to turn round before they meet again, so that the second meeting is head-on. Here both turns happen before the 3-hour mark (at about 1.7 hours and 2.4 hours), so it is safe. If one walker were more than twice as fast as the other, they could catch the slower walker from behind before the slower one reached the end, and the argument would have to change. Here the first meeting shows that the speeds are in the ratio 5 : 7 (5 km and 7 km in the same time), and 7 is less than twice 5, so the shortcut is safe. Checking that the conditions of a shortcut hold is part of using it properly.

**General lesson**

When speeds are steady, distances are proportional to times, so you can reason about times by counting distances in a convenient unit, here the length of the road.

questions.answer: They meet for the second time **3 km from B** (that is, 9 km from A).
